Sports.title: How best to punish City? Restitution over retribution, then hand club to the fans | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
A 17-year transfer embargo. Replay the entire era with all the original players. Restore the 2009 squad and force them to mount a title challenge with Stephen Ireland, Martin Petrov and Richard Dunne. Force Ferran Soriano to drive a parade bus backwards through Manchester, once for every major trophy won. Ban the Poznan, or at least make City fans do it facing forwards.

Yes, in the week since it emerged that Manchester City have been found guilty of all the financial charges laid against them by the Premier League, a great and cathartic silliness has begun to stalk the land. The Sainsbury’s account on Instagram posting a picture that reads “114 unexpected items in the bagging area”. The relentless trolling from Domino’s Pizza, which claims to have “irrefutable evidence that pineapple is the best pizza topping”.

The City fan on BBC 5 Live arguing that the club’s defiance of unfair rules is part of a rich tradition of civil disobedience going back to the suffragettes and the Peterloo massacre, and therefore justified because “they’re trying to massacre Manchester City”. Liam Gallagher’s late-night diatribes on X, the most unhinged of which compares City to “Jesus prepared to die on the cross”. (The most popular reply, naturally, simply reads: “Sham Pain Supernova”.)

And on some level it’s possible to see the ritualistic ridicule of City as the first downpayment on any punishment: a kind of collective healing, banter as therapy. Before the stripping of points and titles, the stripping of dignity. This is always how the British have dealt with anything, from an early general election to the death of a treasured celebrity. I heard my first Princess Diana joke within about 15 seconds of walking through the school gates the following Monday morning.

Back in the real world of real consequences, the Abu Dhabi counteroffensive was beginning in earnest. While City launched their appeal, Etihad Airways was threatening to sue the Premier League for the “damaging implications” of the verdict and government officials from the United Arab Emirates were surreptitiously warning that the case could threaten diplomatic relations and billions of pounds of investment into the UK.

Which sounds like a pretty hefty multi-pronged problem until you realise that these are all basically the same entity. Like one of those one-man stage shows you see at the Edinburgh fringe, where all the characters are played by a single guy scurrying around the stage frenetically putting on different costumes. UAE dignitaries? The leadership of Etihad Airways? The board of Manchester City? Goodness, your versatility astonishes us. That’s acting range for you.

View image in fullscreen One suggestion to start reversing the damage: force Manchester City fans to do the Poznan facing forwards. Photograph: Mike Egerton

Still, all of this is a long-overdue reminder that when you allow state actors to control your football clubs, even the most minor footballing decisions become matters of diplomacy, geopolitics, peace and war. Witness the desperate contortions this week of Andy Burnham, who offered a stiff-armed defence of City’s ownership before belatedly realising that appearing to side with English football’s most notorious cheats may just be the sort of thing that polls badly in certain swing postcodes.

None of which, of course, gets us any closer to a workable solution. And of course you will have your own strong views over what should happen to City, assuming their trail of appeals and grievances is finally exhausted at some point. There are no real precedents here, and so there are no wrong answers. The emotions are still raw. Often it is said that victims should not dispense justice. But what happens when the victim is an entire sport, an entire generation of fans, clubs who lost their best players, broadcasters who as it turned out were pointing their cameras at a sham competition?

These are almost philosophical questions, questions of justice and ethics and morality. Do you decide that the strict imperative is to punish or “cancel” the harm done, as Kant or Hegel might have argued? Do you agree with Durkheim that the point of punishment is not exemplary deterrence but the reinforcement of shared moral values, or with Bentham that the infliction of pain for its own sake simply prolongs the original sin, and that the emphasis should always be on averting future evil? And do any of these scenarios end with Victor Lindelöf lifting a Premier League trophy?

View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham faced pressure this week after defending Manchester City’s owners. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA Wire

What follows here is little more than a personal prospectus, guided above all by two principles. Firstly that the relitigation of history – the messy and unsatisfactory business of reassigning trophies and medals – is an unserious solution for unserious people. Rewriting the past on the basis of a counterfactual is no more feasible than asking the shark to regurgitate, reassemble and reanimate the body of the surfer he has just crunched to pieces. It is one thing to tell the world that what we saw was not real. It is quite another to perpetrate the compound fiction that something entirely different happened instead.

As Jamie Carragher put it so well on Sky Sports this week, winning is less about the silverware and the trinkets than the moments and the memories, the aura of victory and the hangovers the following morning, and those are gone for ever. Carved up, parcelled away. And of course City knew this at the time. The Touré goal, the 6-1 at Old Trafford, the Agüero goal, the Kompany goal: those moments are safe, banked, untouchable. “We know what we felt,” a lot of City fans have been saying in the last few days, and they’re right.

The second principle is that any punishment should seek to inflict maximum punishment on City’s owners and as little as possible on City’s fans. The fans may have shared in the proceeds of cheating, may often have defended the owners in obnoxious and myopic ways, and perhaps it feels purgative and satisfying to throw them under the bus too. But ultimately they too are victims of a grand deception. They too were gaslit, lied to, told the dream was real life. In many ways the subterfuge is all the crueller because of how desperate they were to believe it.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

And so any redress that deprives one of the country’s biggest fanbases of their club, that forces them out of existence, that cuts the body off at the knees and forces it to beg for mercy at the very bottom of the food chain, is also doomed to failure. And let’s be real: this isn’t going to happen in practice. The commercial appeal of Manchester City uplifts the entire league. Broadcast and commercial contracts would need to be redrawn. Ultimately throwing them out of football altogether, kicking them down the stairs, would cost everyone at the top of English football a lot of money. And we know how much they hate that.

But there is a recourse, albeit improbable and outlandish, that fulfils all the criteria of restitution, if not retribution. The new football regulator has the power to strip rogue owners of their position and force them to sell up. This sounds like a good punishment. But market intelligence suggests City are worth about £4bn now, compared with about £200m when the Abu Dhabi United Group took over in 2008. What kind of punishment enables the perpetrators to walk away with a 20-fold profit on their investment, much of which can be attributed to their cheating?

No, City should not be sold; they should be taken back. Requisition. Nationalise. Give them some patriotic name such as the Great British Manchester Football Club. Return Phil Foden to the exchequer. Enzo Maresca, you are now an employee of the UK government. And while this sounds outlandish because it is outlandish, there is a recent precedent here. Chelsea’s operations were briefly controlled by the government after sanctions were imposed on their owner Roman Abramovich and he agreed to offload the club. It was surreal, exceptional and only ever intended as a temporary measure.

View image in fullscreen Manchester city council owns the freehold to the Etihad Stadium. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

There are plenty of levers that can be pulled here, if there is the political will to do so. Manchester city council owns the Etihad Stadium. A report by Tax Policy Associates has suggested that City may owe HMRC as much as £12m in unpaid tax over the Roberto Mancini contract. The cross-party Treasury committee has urged HMRC to scrutinise the findings of the Premier League case. Meanwhile, every week that City stay in their current ownership is a week in which money flows from fans and broadcasters and sponsors into the pockets of Abu Dhabi. No wonder City’s ruling regime has a vested interest in elongating this process as long as possible.

Nobody bats an eyelid at the idea of the state owning a park or a motorway or a museum, or taking over a failing train company or steelworks or bank. In each case there is a recognition that the asset has a broader social value that requires a certain protection against market forces. And of course the longer-term ambition here is not to run Manchester City as an arm of the state, but eventually to give the club back to its people. To gradually assemble the governance structures that would allow fans a genuine voice in the running of their club and facilitate an eventual sale. And in the meantime to maintain one of the country’s most successful football clubs as a going concern, generating revenue that will allow it to pay back its debt to English football.

None of this is going to happen. Abu Dhabi would rather hire the world’s 50 best lawyers to sue Burnham for the next 30 years before it allowed one of its prized assets to be given away for free. But also: is this not what we should want to happen? If any tangible good is to come from the sordid City case beyond memes and banter, perhaps it is a realisation that the ownership model of English football needs to be reimagined on a radical level. That a system built on the wholesale transfer of wealth from fans to owners is exploitation by any other name. That City are not the disease, but the symptom. And that the first rule of politics remains its most crucial: never waste a good crisis.

Sports.title: Manchester City’s England players are worried about their futures, admits Tuchel
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel has suggested Manchester City’s England contingent are worried about the club being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules.

Tuchel, who said he would be prepared to keep picking City players if they were relegated, revealed the case had been a major topic of conversation in the England camp before the Nations League game against Croatia. The head coach said there had been discussions during meals and delivered an honest response after being asked whether the situation had become a distraction.

“If I say now it’s not then I can just speak for myself, which would be totally narrow-minded,” Tuchel said. “I think it is a distraction. It is. Let’s say it is a subject. If it’s a distraction, I don’t know.

“It is of course a topic and we speak about it at dinner and at a table of eight or 12 people. We speak about it at breakfast. I know the Man City players get a lot of messages and phone calls and feedback about it.

“Are they worried or concerned? I think that would be a very human reaction if you don’t know what’s going on for the club that you signed. They’re still young. They’re ambitious. They’re told they are totally innocent and don’t know what’s going on. It is a subject.

“I am again not sure if it’s a distraction. I don’t see it when I see them in my meetings. I don’t see it how they behave with other teammates, and I don’t see it in training being a distraction. But it’s a topic. How can’t it be?”

The Football Association blocked a subsequent question to Tuchel on whether the City case represented a danger to English football. City maintain their innocence and on Friday announced an appeal against the verdict.

For Tuchel, the focus is on his squad. He selected three City players for this camp: Elliot Anderson, Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly, who has withdrawn injured. Guéhi made a costly error during last weekend’s defeat by Spain and Anderson was off colour during the win over Czechia last Tuesday but Tuchel believes both are ready to start against Croatia on Saturday night.

England are second in Group A3 with three points from two games. Jordan Pickford, who remains the No 1, will replace James Trafford in goal and Tuchel must decide whether to restore Jarell Quansah at right-back after Trent Alexander-Arnold shone against Czechia in Prague.

Alexander-Arnold was an unused substitute when England drew in Rijeka in 2018. His place remains uncertain and Tuchel considered whether it was now or never for the Real Madrid defender, who turns 28 next week.

“Maybe, maybe a little bit,” he said. “Once you are in camp it’s a big opportunity if other players are not here. Trent is a unique player. He is not a runner, he is not someone who runs through the last line, who does overlaps, underlaps.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel has said it ‘may be’ now or never for Trent Alexander-Arnold to win his place in the England team. Photograph: Antonio Bronić/Reuters

Tuchel explained that Alexander-Arnold is building a connection with Bukayo Saka. “Bukayo is normally used to a lot of movements around him,” he said. “That brings normally the best out of Bukayo. They need also to find a way to not be too static, to not be too ball-position focused and that we play with dynamic movement. That’s maybe the challenge for Trent: to buy a little bit into a new idea and a bit out of his comfort zone. He’s trying and it’s never too late to prove a point.”

Tuchel is happy with Saka’s level. The Arsenal winger struggled with fitness during the World Cup but has been a regular for his club this season.

“He had a strong start,” Tuchel said. “I could see he was pain-free. He had a bit of a strange ending to last season. He was playing through the pain, he was deciding matches but struggling to have big influence – and yet then having the biggest influence, by scoring decisive goals.

“He scored decisive goals without being fit and without having the capability to accelerate and decelerate. Now I felt him more involved, and felt he was more dangerous at the start of the season – and still I think there is some level still to come when he plays for England.”

Sports.title: Etihad’s statements on funding appear to contradict Manchester City’s defence
Sports.content:
Manchester City’s defence in their appeal against the independent commission’s guilty verdict in more than 100 charges of financial rule breaches appears to be contradicted by previous statements made by their main sponsor, Etihad Airways, to the US government.

A key element of City’s appeal, which was confirmed by the club on Friday, is understood to be based on their claim that commercial contracts, which the commission concluded were part-funded by their owner, were in fact paid for by the Abu Dhabi government.

In a 2015 submission to the United States’ department of commerce, transportation and state as part of investigation into state-owned airlines, Etihad described suggestions that the government paid for its sponsorship of the club as “false”.

Etihad, the state-owned national airline of the United Arab Emirates, has been City’s principal shirt sponsor since 2009 and was the main source of the initial transformation of their revenue that followed their purchase by Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group (Adug) the previous year.

In 2011 City announced a 10-year naming rights deal worth £400m for the Etihad Stadium, which was extended on improved terms in 2021.

The Etihad submission to the US department of commerce said: “The assertion that the Abu Dhabi government paid for Etihad’s sponsorship of English Premier League football club Manchester City is false. In 2011, Etihad and Manchester City entered into a 10-year sponsorship agreement, which included naming rights for Manchester City’s stadium. Etihad funded this sponsorship from its own liquidity.

“We are government-owned and have been since our founding. We are and have always been clear that we do not receive any subsidies from the Abu Dhabi government, and that we are financed through a combination of equity, shareholder and commercial loans.

“Our shareholder [the Abu Dhabi government]’s equity and loans are not subsidies under any applicable definition; they are the means by which the Abu Dhabi government has sensibly invested in a successful business model.”

City’s argument is also a departure from the position the club took in their successful appeal against Uefa’s charges of breaching financial fair play rules at the court of arbitration for sport in 2020, when they maintained that all their sponsorship income was provided by their commercial partners.

The commission dismissed City’s argument as “untrue” in its core decision published on Tuesday. Paragraph 77 of the judgment states: “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme.” City submitted their appeal on Thursday evening and insist they have “a body of irrefutable evidence” that will prove the commission’s findings to be untrue.

The Football Association has confirmed it has powers to take disciplinary action against City and key individuals at the club. The FA said the independent commission’s decision on City had “significant implications for the integrity of the game” and that it “will take action where appropriate”.

The FA will wait until the appeal process has concluded – which based on the Premier League’s rule book should be by the end of January – before deciding whether to take action but said it was monitoring the case closely.

The FA has powers to take action against individuals proved to have broken rules and/or acted dishonestly, which the commission concluded had been the case. The names of those involved were redacted in the 40-page core judgment published this week but the FA could ask the Premier League for an unredacted version.

“The Independent Commission’s decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game,” the FA statement read. “We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.

Quick Guide How do I 

“As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely.”

The FA’s standard practice is to wait for disciplinary proceedings conducted by leagues, such as the Premier League or EFL, to run their course before taking action.

In July the FA fined Chelsea £10m and imposed a suspended two-window transfer ban after the club admitted 74 breaches of its agent regulations, four months after the Premier League fined them £10.75m for the same offences, which related to unlawful payments to players and agents. The FA has additional powers to take action against individuals, although did not do so in the Chelsea case because those involved are no longer working in football.

The FA charged Southampton’s manager, Tonda Eckert, with misconduct for his role in the so-called Spygate saga involving Middlesbrough in May, with a disciplinary hearing taking place last month that could result in the German being given a lengthy ban from football.

Sports.title: Nations League: Italy earn draw against 10-man France, Northern Ireland stun Ukraine
Sports.content:
Zinedine Zidane’s first home game in charge of France ended with a 1-1 draw against Italy in the Nations League on Friday. Visiting keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma produced a string of saves to frustrate fans at Stade de France, while the hosts ended the game with 10 men after Dayot Upamecano’s late dismissal.

Michael Olise put France ahead in the 55th minute with a curling shot that went in off the crossbar, following a short free-kick taken by Rayan Cherki. But poor defending midway through the second half allowed Italy defender Alessandro Bastoni to run through and clip a low shot inside the right post.

Moise Kean missed a close-range chance early on for Italy, shooting straight at goalkeeper Mike Maignan. Donnarumma made a double save from Ousmane Dembélé and Désiré Doué early in the second half, then produced a brilliant low save to deny Adrien Rabiot moments after Italy’s equaliser.

Upamecano was sent off late in the game for picking up a second yellow card, but the hosts kept pushing for a winner, and Donnarumma had to claw away Eduardo Camavinga’s shot in stoppage time to preserve a point.

“We would have liked to win for our fans tonight but I was obviously really touched and delighted to be back at the Stade de France,” Zidane said afterwards. “I am happy with the performance albeit not with the result. We had chances to score a second goal and we didn’t do it. But I am really proud of my players.”

The Italy manager, Roberto Mancini, was pleased with his side’s efforts. “I think this was a great performance tonight against one of the best teams in the world, with very positive aspects to it,” he said. “We are on the right road, and we need to keep playing this way.”

France stay top of Group A1, a point clear of Belgium who eased to a 3-0 home win over bottom side Turkey in Liège. The two neighbours meet again on Monday at the Stade de France, while Italy host Turkey in Bologna.

View image in fullscreen Kevin De Bruyne celebrates after scoring one of his two goals for Belgium in Liège. Photograph: Virginie Lefour/Belga/Shutterstock

Kevin De Bruyne, in his 127th match for the Red Devils, scored the opening goal with a cool finish from the edge of the box, after a nice one-two with Dodi Lukebakio. Turkey posed the greater attacking danger after the Napoli midfielder’s opener but could not find a leveller and were punished just before the hour mark.

De Bruyne claimed his second goal in the 59th minute, curling a ball from the edge of the box past Turkey goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir into the top corner. Romelu Lukaku, Belgium’s all-time record goalscorer, added a third in the 76th minute, skewing the ball home from Charles De Ketelaere’s low cross.

In League B, Northern Ireland stunned Ukraine 3-0 in Slovakia to go clear at the top of their group and boost their hopes of promotion to the top tier.

Ciaron Brown, the only player in Michael O’Neill’s starting lineup over the age of 24, scored twice either side of Isaac Price’s goal in Trnava. The away win puts Northern Ireland on seven points from three games, and they are still yet to concede going into Monday’s clash with Georgia in Belfast.

Northern Ireland’s positive start was quickly rewarded as Kieran Morrison floated a corner to the back post where Ruairi McConville headed it back for Brown, earning his 33rd cap, to prod home despite the desperate efforts of Illia Zabarnyi on the line.

View image in fullscreen Ciaron Brown (left, No 22) celebrates his second goal of the night in Trnava. Photograph: Dénes Erdős/AP

Georgiy Sudakov was the first Ukraine player to get a sight of goal but his 19th-minute effort was straight at keeper Pierce Charles, and moments later the hosts were 2-0 down. Morrison’s first-time ball into the box was met powerfully by Price at the back post – earning Morrison an assist in his first competitive international.

Brown’s second came in bizarre fashion just after the hour – the 28-year-old Oxford defender went up to flick on Pierce Charles’ free-kick from inside the Northern Ireland half, and Ukraine goalkeeper Dmytro Riznyk let the bouncing ball slip through his legs to wrap up a remarkable result.

“It’s a great result for us, a great performance,” O’Neill said. “The early goal helps settle us into the game. The second goal was a brilliant goal. We worked it the length of the pitch. We were patient. We could have crossed it early but that allowed us to get more men in the box and it’s a brilliant header from Isaac.

“The third goal is fortuitous but it’s a mistake by the opposition, so we have to capitalise on that, but I thought throughout our performance was brilliant,” the Northern Ireland manager added. “We limited the opposition to crosses and shots from outside the box and I thought we defended brilliantly.”

The Liverpool full-back Milos Kerkez scored the only goal in the other Group B2 tie to earn Hungary a 1-0 win over Georgia, moving the Magyars level with Ukraine in second place with four points from three games.

Edin Dzeko brought the curtain down on his international career during Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 1-1 draw with Sweden. The 40-year-old was withdrawn after 63 minutes of his 152nd appearance, with the hosts trailing after Viktor Gyökeres had scored two minutes earlier. Kerim Alajbegovic ensured the spoils would be shared with an 80th-minute effort.

In the group’s other game, Poland thumped Romania 6-0 with Robert Lewandowski hitting a hat-trick. Radu Dragusin was sent off in the 22nd minute for bringing Lewandowski down in the area, and the veteran striker got up to convert the penalty. Lewandowski struck again in the 47th and 86th minutes, with Piotr Zielinski, Jan Bednarek and a Virgil Ghita own goal completing the scoring in Warsaw.

View image in fullscreen Robert Lewandowski scores from the penalty spot to kick off Poland’s 6-0 rout of Romania. Photograph: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

The Faroe Islands earned an impressive 1-1 home draw with Group C3 leaders Slovakia, Adrian Justinussen’s second-half goal cancelling out a Gunnar Vatnhamar own goal before the break. Moldova moved up to second in the group with a 2-1 away victory over Kazakhstan.

Elsewhere in the third tier, Vasilije Adzic scored twice as Group C2 leaders Montenegro won 2-1 in Latvia, while Cyprus beat Armenia 2-0 despite a second-half red card for Kostas Pileas.

Sports.title: Arsenal shelve plans for major expansion of Emirates Stadium
Sports.content:
Arsenal have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium, opting for a programme of smaller improvements as the club’s owners review the Premier League champions’ wider operation.

Arsenal set up a working group led by the chief executive, Richard Garlick, in 2024 to examine the feasibility of increasing the 60,704 capacity, with some reports they could temporarily hold home matches at Wembley. But the club has decided against major redevelopment and will concentrate on what it described as the “continued evolution” of their home since 2006.

Arsenal confirmed at a supporters’ meeting that improvements would focus on hospitality, retail, visitor facilities and the matchday experience – an area the co-chair Josh Kroenke previously highlighted.

“We shared a commitment to the continued evolution of Emirates Stadium, rather than a huge-scale masterplan, building on improvement we have made to date in partnership with our catering partner, Legends, the introduction of safe standing (this season in the Clock End, and next season in the North Bank), improving hospitality and retail experiences, and upgrading visitor experiences,” Arsenal said.

Mikel Arteta, who last season guided Arsenal to their first Premier League title since 2022, is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would have been caused by any temporary move. It is understood Arsenal did not apply to host matches at Euro 2028, with a potential redevelopment in mind.

The club’s owner, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, which agreed a record $4bn deal to buy Major League Baseball’s Los Angeles Angels last month, is understood to have brought in Boston Consulting Group (BCG) to examine parts of the operations. The review is understood to be overseen internally by Garlick and to be ongoing.

There is no indication the review will necessarily result in job losses among Arsenal’s approximately 800 employees. Sources have suggested the work is principally focused on non-football operations and identifying ways to improve efficiency.

The decision over the Emirates comes amid competition from Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which opened in 2019 with a capacity of 62,850 and was designed to host a wide range of sporting and entertainment events, including NFL games and concerts. Arsenal, despite a smaller capacity, have significantly increased their matchday revenue. Income has reportedly doubled over five seasons to more than £150m a season, helped by the club’s return to the Champions League and an expansion of corporate hospitality.
