World.title: Mineral water springs: 3 levels that set property value
World.content:
My previous article explained why Hungary’s geothermal and mineral water resources represent untapped natural capital and why property prices do not yet reflect their full potential. This article moves one step closer: it examines how a water-law permit and official recognition as natural mineral water can affect the value of a specific property, and why two neighbouring plots that appear identical may command very different prices simply because one is associated with an officially recognised, lawfully exploitable source and the other is not. The value of a property with mineral water springs is shaped not only by market demand, but also by the combination of permits, official recognition and restrictions on use.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

Recognition as natural mineral water: a condition for market access

Natural mineral water is not merely a quality category; it is a legally regulated designation. In Hungary, the Government Office of the Capital City Budapest recognises water as natural mineral water, on application, under Joint Decree 65/2004 (IV. 27.) FVM–ESzCsM–GKM. Only water recognised through this procedure may be marketed under the designation “natural mineral water”. Recognition requires evidence of compliance with the prescribed chemical, microbiological, source-protection, extraction and bottling conditions.

It is not an exclusive market right or a legal monopoly. Rather, recognition is a condition for the lawful use of the designation and for placing the product on the market, while the geological characteristics of the source and the site-specific permits may create commercial scarcity.

According to the case files available to me, hydrodynamic modelling for one of the sources examined demonstrated an adequate degree of protection for the water base, while tritium analysis supported the conclusion that the water originated in deeper strata. The Government Office of the Capital City Budapest recognised the water as natural mineral water. That recognition, together with the relevant water-law permits and protection measures, may have substantial market value, but it does not create a statutory monopoly.

The Börzsöny case: mineral water springs, 150 metres and a decade-long process

I know the case of a mineral water source in the Börzsöny hills well. According to the documentation available to me, the well was drilled in 1979 to a depth of approximately 150 metres and produces high-quality aquifer water. Hydrodynamic modelling was prepared for the operating permit, using numerical simulation to examine the vulnerability of the water base and the origin of the water. Over the 50-year assessment horizon, the model indicated no recharge from surface sources; the calculation used a recharge zone with a radius of 448 metres, and the tritium content was negligible.

Official recognition of the water as natural mineral water, together with the completion of the related permitting process, materially strengthened the property’s market position. The point at which the recognition decision became final was the key legal milestone affecting value.

The protection system as both a value driver and a constraint

The protection of water bases is governed by Government Decree 123/1997 (VII. 18.). The system provides for inner and outer subsurface protection zones, hydrogeological zones A, B and C, and corresponding surface protection areas where a subsurface zone reaches the surface. The inner protection zone must be designated. Whether outer and hydrogeological A and B surface protection areas must also be designated depends in part on whether the corresponding subsurface zones reach the surface, while a hydrogeological C zone is not mandatory in every case.

Not every restriction appears on the land-registry title sheet. Inner and outer surface protection areas must be entered in the land register, while rights, obligations and prohibitions associated with hydrogeological protection zones are also recorded in the water-law register (vízikönyvi nyilvántartás). The protection system may restrict certain uses of surrounding land while reducing the risk of contamination of the water base.

A source with a properly established protection system may therefore embody two forms of value. The first is the verified water use authorised by a valid operating water-law permit. Ownership of the property and entitlement under the permit do not necessarily belong to the same person, however, and purchasing the property does not automatically transfer the permit. A change in the permit holder or the owner may require an authority review and an amendment to the permit. The second source of value is the protection of the water base, which may restrict certain uses of neighbouring properties and thereby help preserve water quality over the long term.

The Great Plain case: value held in suspension

A different situation arises where the resource exists, the well has been drilled and the water has been chemically tested, but exploitation has not begun. I am also closely familiar with a thermal well on the Great Hungarian Plain. It draws thermal water from a depth of nearly 950 metres at a temperature above 50 °C. According to the laboratory report available to me, its silicic-acid content, expressed as SiO2, is approximately 341 mg/l, nearly four times the silica content of Fiji Water, a frequently cited global premium benchmark.

The chemical profile alone, however, does not establish eligibility for recognition as natural mineral water or medicinal water, nor does it demonstrate suitability for beverage or therapeutic use. Separate testing and authority procedures are required. The well has not operated since it was drilled in 2007, not because of its geological characteristics, but because parallel permitting procedures became protracted.

This is a case in which the theoretical value of a property associated with mineral water springs or a thermal water resource may be high, while the market price does not yet reflect it. From an investment perspective, this may be the entry point, but only for a buyer who understands what is required to turn geological promise into a legally exploitable asset.

What is a spring actually worth in the property price?

The answer depends on the stage reached in the permitting and recognition process. The following three levels are not statutory categories, but a practical due-diligence model.

Level one: speculative. The presence of the water resource is suspected on geological grounds or has been documented, but no valid authority permit exists; any water-related premium is therefore largely speculative. Level two: permitted but not recognised. The well has been completed and has a valid operating water-law permit, but the recognition procedure required for the intended commercial or therapeutic use has not yet been completed. Level three: fully resolved. The relevant recognition decision has become final, the applicable subsurface protection zone or surface protection area has been designated, and all permits required for the intended bottling or other use are in place.

At that third stage, the property’s value can be assessed according to a different logic from that applied to ordinary land or buildings.

What comes next

Reaching the third level requires a complex process involving several authorities and overlapping fields of law. The next article examines this path in detail, including the roles of the regional water-management and water-protection authority, the mining authority where applicable, and the nature-conservation, agricultural-land-protection, building and land-registry bodies; it also considers Natura 2000 implications and the long-term sustainability of permits, drawing on direct experience of the two projects described here.

Legislation cited

This article provides general market and legal information only and does not constitute individual legal, water-law or food-law advice. The project-specific data described above should be verified against the original laboratory reports, permits and authority decisions. The English titles of Hungarian legislation are descriptive translations; the Hungarian-language legal text is authoritative. Legislation checked as at 3 September 2026.

World.title: Danube water levels could fall way below 200-year low
World.content:
The Danube has fallen to a historic low in Budapest, with water levels expected to decline further over the weekend as persistent dry weather continues across the river’s catchment area.

What do negative water levels mean?

On Wednesday, the Budapest water gauge recorded -1 centimetre, breaking a record that had stood for almost 200 years. The level had previously fallen to zero in early September, but continued drought has since pushed the river below that mark.

The gauge’s zero point corresponds to the lowest water level recorded during the 1834 low-water period. A negative reading does not mean that the riverbed is dry; rather, it indicates that the water level has fallen below the historic reference point.

Regular state measurements in Budapest began in 1823, and the river had never previously fallen below today’s zero mark. According to water-management authorities, the latest reading therefore represents an unprecedented low in the modern measurement record.

Danube water levels are expected to decline even further

Hungary’s General Directorate of Water Management predicts that the situation could deteriorate further, with the Danube potentially reaching -8 centimetres in Budapest by the weekend. The continuing lack of rainfall across the river’s catchment area is the main factor behind the decline. Little significant precipitation is expected in the Alps and along the upper reaches of the Danube, meaning there is currently no clear source of increased water flow, writes Időkép.

The effects are being felt elsewhere in Hungary as well. At Paks, the river could fall to around -113 centimetres, although an earlier record low of -140 centimetres is not currently expected to be challenged. A riverbed threshold constructed there in August has helped maintain water levels.

The exceptionally low conditions are also creating growing difficulties for river navigation, as sandbanks and obstacles on the riverbed come increasingly close to the surface. With little rainfall forecast, Budapest and other sections of the Danube may continue to experience unusually low water levels in the coming days.

World.title: Major step for the Hungarian minority in Ukraine as educational bill submitted to parliament
World.content:
Ukraine has taken a significant legislative step towards strengthening the educational rights of its Hungarian minority, submitting a bill to parliament that would expand protections for minority-language schooling. The move has been welcomed by Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, although the legislation still needs parliamentary approval.

The bill, registered in Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada on 1 October, is expected to be considered later this month. It follows a June agreement between Budapest and Kyiv concerning the linguistic, educational and cultural rights of Hungary’s ethnic Hungarian community in Ukraine.

What would change?

Under the proposed legislation, Ukrainian would remain the language of the education system. However, schools with classes or groups teaching in the language of an indigenous people or an EU-official minority language would be guaranteed the right to use that language. The bill would also create a formal status for secondary schools serving national minorities. Institutions where more than half of pupils receive education in a minority language could qualify for this status.

For Hungarian-speaking pupils, the proposed framework could allow schools to teach national history and preserve elements of their material and cultural heritage, including traditions, symbols and customs. Official educational documents could also be issued in the minority language at parents’ request. Parents would have the right to request an expansion of subjects taught in Ukrainian, provided that at least two-thirds of parents in the relevant class or group submit a written request.

A dispute stretching back years

Minority-language education has been one of the principal sources of tension between Budapest and Kyiv since Ukraine introduced changes to its language and education policies in the late 2010s. The June 2026 agreement was reached following several weeks of expert-level negotiations involving Hungarian and Ukrainian officials, as well as representatives of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia. The details of the agreement were not initially published, but its stated objective was to expand linguistic, educational and cultural rights.

The issue has also become linked to Ukraine’s European Union accession process. Hungary had previously opposed the opening of parts of the negotiations, while Magyar has said that progress on minority rights is a condition for Budapest’s support for further steps. Reuters reported that Ukraine’s latest bill is therefore closely connected to efforts to advance the accession process.

Budapest welcomes the move

Anita Orbán said the bill followed recent bilateral consultations and discussions with representatives of the Transcarpathian Hungarian community. Magyar likewise said it would strengthen the legal guarantees surrounding Hungarian-language education and the network of educational institutions.

The legislation nevertheless marks only the next stage of the process. Its final wording could still change during parliamentary debate, and its practical impact will depend on how the new provisions are implemented. For the Hungarian-speaking community in Ukraine, the parliamentary process will therefore be closely watched as a test of whether the commitments made in recent months become lasting legal protections.

The new government also drew the line

Speaking to Bloomberg, deputy foreign minister and state secretary György Velkey shared the new government, just like the previous one, won’t send neither soldiers nor military equipment to Ukraine. Despite the Tisza government’s efforts to join the mainstream of the European Union, the EU and especially the Baltic states’ – due to the closeness of Russia – decided to fully support Ukraine against the Russian invasion. Velkey said they believe it is of utmost importance to guarantee peace within Hungary’s borders, hence their support consists of humanitarian aid and energy supply, not weapons and ammunition.

World.title: Revolut users in Hungary face new restriction from December: currency exchanges could be suspended!
World.content:
Revolut will introduce new terms in December, allowing it to temporarily suspend currency exchanges in exceptional market or technical circumstances, potentially affecting some transfers as well.

Revolut users will face a new provision from 3 December 2026 that could temporarily suspend currency exchanges in exceptional circumstances, according to information sent to customers and reported by Bankmonitor.

The new provision will be added to Revolut’s personal terms and conditions. It allows the service to suspend the exchange of certain currencies in situations including extreme exchange-rate movements, liquidity constraints, unavailable exchange rates, or technical or system failures outside Revolut’s control.

The change does not mean that every significant weakening of the Hungarian forint would automatically trigger a suspension. The provision specifically concerns exceptional market and technical circumstances. If a currency temporarily becomes unavailable, Revolut says customers will be informed through the app. However, the new terms do not specify how long such a suspension could last.

Some transfers could also be affected

The restriction could extend beyond straightforward currency exchanges. According to the detailed terms, transfers between Revolut customers that require a currency conversion could also be affected. For example, if someone wanted to send euros to another Revolut user after converting Hungarian forints, the transfer could fail while the relevant currency exchange was suspended.

The change does not, however, mean that Revolut accounts would be frozen or that all transfers would automatically be stopped.

The potential disruption could be particularly inconvenient for customers who need to make an urgent foreign-currency payment. This could include paying for accommodation abroad or settling an invoice issued in euros. If the required currency cannot be exchanged at the time, customers may have to use another payment method or wait until the exchange becomes available again.

A second bank account could provide a backup

Maintaining another bank account alongside Revolut could provide an alternative if a service becomes temporarily unavailable. However, simply having a second account is of limited use if there is no accessible money in it.

Customers who already know they will have expenses in euros could consider exchanging and setting aside the required amount in advance. This could reduce their reliance on currency exchange being available at the exact time a payment is due.

Other banks can also experience service outages or market-related restrictions, so a second account is not a guarantee against disruption. Having accessible funds with more than one provider can nevertheless provide an additional payment option if one service is temporarily unavailable.

Have you heard? Revolut Hungary set to enter ATM market – what will change for customers?

Check foreign-exchange fees before choosing a backup

Anyone considering opening another bank account should look beyond promotional offers and monthly fees. The costs of currency exchange and foreign-currency transfers can be particularly important for customers who regularly make payments in euros or other foreign currencies. A cheap or free Hungarian forint account does not necessarily offer favourable exchange rates or low fees for foreign-currency transactions.

Customers should therefore check how long promotional conditions remain valid, what fees apply afterwards, and what exchange rates and charges are used for foreign-currency transactions.

World.title: Biljana Plavsic, Bosnian Serb War Criminal Who Withdrew Her Remorse
World.content:
The Serb political elites do not recognise the legitimacy of the ICTY and believe, as Plavsic did, that the court was set up “to prosecute Serbs”. Lack of recognition of the court as a legitimate, bipartisan institution has led to many high-ranking war criminals returning to Serbia and being welcomed as heroes, and/or buried with the highest state honours.

Plavsic never changed her convictions. In her now infamous statement of guilt at the ICTY, she apologised for the persecution of “thousands of non-Serbs” during her sentencing hearing in 2002. “I have now come to the belief and accept the fact that many thousands of innocent people were the victims of an organised, systematic effort to remove Muslims and Croats from the territory claimed by Serbs,” she said.

“Although I was repeatedly informed of allegations of cruel and inhuman conduct against non-Serbs, I refused to accept them or even to investigate. The knowledge that I am responsible for such human suffering and for soiling the character of my people will always be with me,” she added.

But, two years later, in an interview from her prison cell in Sweden, Plavsic withdrew her expression of remorse, saying she had done “nothing wrong”. Her denial of any responsibility for the crimes she was convicted of was met with outrage on behalf of victims’ organisations and the international community.

Although Plavsic may be buried with honours in Republika Srpska, she remains a controversial figure among some Serbs because she was the only high-ranking Serb leader who expressed remorse. Some have not forgiven her for this move.

“She should have never apologised and admitted that Serbs committed crimes,” I was told by some of Plavsic’s close acquaintances during my research. I think the backlash Plavsic received from Serbs after her infamous statement of guilt made her adamant in denying it and ultimately withdrawing her remorse. My impression was that she had a strong urge to go down in history as unrepentant.

To regain the image she had lost because of her unpopular expression of remorse, she repeatedly insisted that she did not regret anything she was accused of. On the contrary, she told me on many occasions, “I would do the same again. I had to protect my people. If I contributed anything in establishing Republika Srpska, our Serb state, and I know I did, there is nothing to regret.”

But although she has been called one of the “founders of Republika Srpska”, Plavsic is no longer a household name for the post-war generations of Serbs like her compatriots Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic – who never apologised for their crimes.

Olivera Simic is a professor at Griffith Law School, Griffith University, Australia. She is the author of the book ‘Madam War Criminal: Biljana Plavsic, Serbia’s Iron Lady’, published by Hurst, 2025.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Week in Review: Elections and Struggles
World.content:
As Bosnia and Herzegovina heads to the polls, promises of political renewal are colliding with entrenched habits that cut across party lines. The governing Trojka [Trio] has struggled to deliver the clean break from clientelism and politicised institutions it promised, potentially opening a path back to power for the unreformed main Bosniak party, the Party of Democratic Action, SDA – less through renewed enthusiasm for the party than from voter disappointment and apathy.

Women’s participation in politics is another key issue. Although women account for more than 40 per cent of candidates as a result of legal obligations, they head just 15.5 per cent of the electoral lists, with parties often placing them low down, where their chances of winning are slim.

World.title: Tributes Paid on Sarajevo’s Streets as Edin Dzeko Plays Final Bosnia Match
World.content:
More than a decade later, Dzeko was part of the team that secured Bosnia and Herzegovina’s second World Cup qualification, earning a place at the 2026 tournament. He reached his 150th international appearance during the group stage.

His 73 international goals include 26 in World Cup qualifying, 14 in European Championship qualifying, nine in the UEFA Nations League and two at World Cup finals.

Dzeko acknowledged that the occasion would be difficult for him personally but stressed that the match remained a competitive fixture rather than a farewell exhibition.

“It will be a difficult match for me personally but in the end everything is about the national team. We know it will be a difficult game. Sweden have been returning to their best in recent months, and you can see the progress under the new coach. They know what they are doing and that is why they have six points from two matches. It will be a difficult game for us, but for them as well,” Dzeko said.

World.title: Police From Three Continents Test Anti-Riot Tactics in Romania
World.content:
More than 500 riot police and gendarmerie personnel from 19 countries gathered at the Romanian Gendarmerie’s training centre in Ochiuri this week to act out security-crisis scenarios in which they tested tactics to quell angry rioters throwing projectiles, setting up barricades and attacking public buildings.

The Carpathian Blue Shield 2026 exercise was designed to test joint responses to complex security situations, including coordination, information-sharing and tactical intervention. Participants included forces from Ukraine, Moldova, Bulgaria and the US as well as Western European countries.

Romanian Interior Minister Catalin Predoiu said security risks “are becoming increasingly interconnected”, which requires public-order forces to adapt and train for real-world scenarios involving multiple threats.

World.title: Polish Activists Open the World’s First Parcel-Locker Machine for Abortion Pills
World.content:
Women Help Women, an international abortion-support network, this week unveiled the Abortomat, which it describes as the world’s first parcel-locker machine for abortion pills. It stands inside AboTak, an abortion-support clinic that opened opposite the Polish parliament in the spring of 2025.

The idea behind it is simple: make getting abortion pills closer to picking up an ordinary delivery. Poland has one of Europe’s densest networks of automated parcel lockers. More than 66,700 machines were operating across the country by the end of 2025 – roughly one for every 560 people – collecting clothes, books, groceries and whatever else people order online.

“Parcel lockers are everywhere in Poland – people joke about our ‘paczkoza’, our obsession with them,” Kinga Jelinska, director of Women Help Women, told BIRN. “So why not use that same technology for abortion pills, where getting them to someone faster can actually matter?”

The process involves a person contacting Women Help Women online and, after a consultation, receiving a six-digit code. That code opens one of 22 compartments containing the medication. The machine was designed by engineers and IT specialists commissioned by the organisation and, unlike commercial parcel lockers, does not store users’ personal data, Jelinska explained.

“Sometimes even waiting a few days can be too long,” she said. “For people whose health is at risk, or who are further along in pregnancy, every day really matters.”

In Poland, that wait exists partly because abortion care remains caught between a restrictive legal system and an extensive informal network built to work around it. Abortion is legal only when a pregnancy threatens a woman’s life or health, or results from a criminal act. Helping someone obtain an abortion outside those circumstances can be punishable by up to three years in prison under Article 152 of the criminal code. The pregnant person however is not criminally liable for ending their own pregnancy.

Donald Tusk’s governing coalition came to power in 2023 promising to change the law, but reform has repeatedly stalled. A bill partially decriminalising assistance in abortion has remained in a special parliamentary committee since 2024. In the meantime, activists have filled much of the gap. Abortion Without Borders, a network of Polish and international groups, says it supported 38,508 abortions in 2025, making it the largest de facto abortion care provider in Poland.

The Abortomat pushes that parallel system one step further – and tests the legal boundary surrounding it. “The person collecting the pills is not committing a crime, and the machine itself cannot be prosecuted,” Justyna Wydrzynska of Abortion Dream Team, the collective that runs the Warsaw clinic, said at the launch.

Wydrzynska has personal experience of that boundary. In 2023, she was convicted of assisting an abortion after sending pills to a woman who had sought help during the Covid pandemic. An appeals court later overturned the conviction and ordered a retrial.

Some lawyers are unconvinced that putting a machine between the activist and the person taking the pills changes much. “Assistance can cover a very broad range of actions,” criminal lawyer Pawel Matyja told Polish news outlet Zero.pl, arguing that sending the medication, arranging its collection and providing the access code could together still amount to assisting an abortion. “These are essentially a series of steps without which the woman would not be able to have the abortion.”

For the time being, the Abortomat will remain indoors for security reasons, Jelinska said. She would much rather put it outside, but since AboTak opened, anti-abortion protesters have regularly gathered outside its entrance. Some demonstrations have involved loudspeakers and vuvuzelas, while the premises have also been targeted with butyric acid.

“Our aim is to draw attention to an institution operating in the heart of the capital which, in our view, violates Polish law. We will continue protesting until it is closed,” Laura Lipinska of the Zycie i Rodzina Foundation, which participates in the protests, said in a statement after the centre opened in 2025.

Despite the protests and legal uncertainty, the activists are pressing ahead. “If we worried about what might happen, or how people might react,” Jelinska said, “we wouldn’t have done anything for the past 12 years.”

World.title: After Bosnia’s ‘Anaemic’ Election Campaign, Polling Day Sees New Challenge
World.content:
On Saturday, the day before Bosnians vote in general elections, election officials in some 5,700 polling stations are due to switch on scanners and fingerprint readers that most of the country has never used before. This is to run tests and so determine whether the technology works properly.

“It is a logistical challenge,” Tihana Bartulec Blanc, president of the US-based NGO Civic Hub and a veteran international election observer, told BIRN.

BIRN spoke to three experts about the impact of the nationwide debut of biometric voter checks and ballot scanners, which arrives in a campaign that analysts otherwise describe as lacklustre.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Operation Purgatory Snares Former Hungarian Ministers
World.content:
Fico juggles jobs and coalition; another fatal school attack shocks Slovakia

Robert Fico is currently Slovakia’s prime minister and, temporarily, its environment minister. The second job may prove easier than keeping his three-party coalition together. On Wednesday, President Peter Pellegrini handed the environment portfolio to Fico after dismissing Tomas Taraba. Taraba’s increasingly bitter feud with Slovak National Party (SNS) leader Andrej Danko culminated in an unprecedented episode in Slovakia’s recent political history: SNS MPs joining the opposition in voting to remove a minister nominated by their own party, after Fico had rejected a request to dismiss Taraba. The minister’s exit resolves one problem but leaves Fico with a larger one. Back in parliament as an independent MP, Taraba says he remains loyal to Fico, but will decide on how to vote on a case-by-case basis. With 76 votes needed for a majority, the government has little room for such conditional loyalty – particularly with the 2027 budget due in October. If parliament fails to approve it, Slovakia would enter a provisional budget regime, limiting monthly spending to one-twelfth of the current year’s budget. The coalition reckons it has 78 MPs, but that number could fall on individual votes. There is no obvious replacement for Taraba either. SNS claims the Environment Ministry under the coalition agreement and wants Deputy Environment Minister Filip Kuffa, though Taraba himself has questioned Kuffa’s qualifications. Kuffa has also faced criticism from the opposition in the past. The turmoil revived speculation about an early election, an option Fico himself recently put on the table. For now, however, the three coalition parties have strong reasons to keep the government alive. SNS is polling below the threshold for entering parliament, while coalition partner Hlas opposes an early vote, saying it has yet to deliver everything it promised its voters. Fico also has major projects and unfinished legislative business he may want to see through. Moreover, ending parliament’s term requires 90 MPs, meaning the coalition would also need opposition votes. At this point, an early election remains possible, though not probable. Fico and his Smer party have survived bigger challenges in the past, most notably in 2018 after the murder of investigative journalist Jan Kuciak and his fiancee, Martina Kusnirova, and subsequent mass protests. Fico resigned as prime minister, but Smer remained in government until the 2020 election.

Slovakia is again confronting violence in its schools this week after a 13-year-old boy killed a teacher and a classmate in the northern village of Staskov, northern Slovakia. Bozena Mariakova, 61, and the unnamed female pupil died after the boy attacked them with a knife. He also seriously wounded another teacher, whose condition is now reported as being stable. The boy has been placed in a psychological detention facility. At 13, he cannot be held criminally responsible under Slovak law. What happened before the attack is now under scrutiny. Days earlier, the murdered girl had reportedly alerted teachers to an image created by the boy showing a concentration camp with teachers’ faces. He could have had his conduct grade lowered over the incident. Psychologists spent two hours with his class on Monday, while the school had also filed a criminal complaint with police five days before the attack. Police are now reviewing how local officers dealt with that complaint. Little is publicly known about the boy. Residents told Slovak media he was being raised by his grandmother and mentioned unspecified difficulties involving his mother. A woman who knew him from church remembered him as a bright boy who served at Mass and read well, but rarely appeared cheerful. The attack comes less than two years after a student killed two people at a school in Spisska Stara Ves, eastern Slovakia. It also coincides with parliament debating a government bill on preventing radicalisation and mobilisation to violence among young people.

World.title: Zadar Connected Year-Round: Winter Flights to Munich Confirmed, Expansion to Paris, London or Venice
World.content:
October the 3rd, 2026 – Zadar is set to become connected year-round, with winter flights to Munich now confirmed, and expansion to Paris, London or Venice being actively eyed.

The new year-round air route between Zadar and Munich should be only the beginning of the further expansion of Zadar’s air connectivity with Europe, County Prefect Josip Bilaver said in response to journalists’ questions after a working meeting at the Zadar County House with Croatian Roads Management Board President Ivica Budimir and associates. O23 reports how Bilaver recalled that the possibility of introducing a year-round connection was announced about a year ago, and that operations during the winter months have now also been confirmed. He emphasised that the first reactions from citizens have been extremely positive.

“Munich is a major international air hub from which you can continue travelling practically to the entire world. Our wish is to have more such routes and we believe this should only be the beginning,” Bilaver said. He added that talks have already been held with other airlines, as well as with Croatia Airlines, and that further expansion of the year-round route offer is expected next year.

“As a county, together with the tourist boards, cities and municipalities and the tourism sector, we are ready to support such projects. Representatives of the tourism sector already several months ago expressed their readiness to participate in co-financing the routes. When we have concrete routes and proposals, we will also discuss concrete amounts,” the Prefect announced. He stressed that year-round air connectivity is important not only for tourism, but also for better connecting the residents of Zadar County with the rest of Europe and indeed the world.

“A good indicator will be precisely the Munich route, for which we expect good occupancy. After that we will see whether there is a possibility of connecting Zadar with some other major European centre. Split, for example, has a connection with Rome, but I believe there is no need for us to compete with them on the same route in the winter period. I would like Zadar to get a connection with some other major European centre such as Venice, Paris or London and thus further expand its year-round connectivity,” County Prefect Bilaver concluded.

World.title: Railway Mega-Project Would Position Croatia as Important Transit Hub
World.content:
October the 3rd, 2026 – The recently announced and sighed railway mega-project has a high chance of positioning Croatia as an important transit hub.

The future Adriatic-Ionian railway corridor would bring many benefits, and its importance is also recognised by the European Commission. Europe must be better connected, that’s the premise that guided the signatories of the initiative “Adriatic-Ionian Railway Corridor. Transport Connectivity is deemed to be the Foundation of Development and Resilience”, and finalising the documents, the first step has been taken towards a future railway corridor that will connect Italy, Slovenia and Croatia with Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Albania and Greece. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that Croatia could benefit greatly in this story, as the new corridor would specifically link Trieste, Koper, Rijeka, Zadar, Šibenik, Split, Ploče, Bar, Durrës and Greek centres along the Adriatic-Ionian route.

better connectivity for all

The initiative was signed on Friday by Member of the European Parliament and member of the Committee on Transport and Tourism Nikolina Brnjac, Zadar County Prefect Josip Bilaver, representatives of the coastal counties, and State Secretary in the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure Žarko Tušek. The aim of the initiative, it was said at the conference, is to better connect Croatia by rail with neighbouring countries and the rest of the Adriatic-Ionian region and to encourage joint investments in transport infrastructure, Hina reports.

“I don’t even need to say how important this is for the railway connection of Ploče, the Port of Ploče, with the ports of Split, Zadar, Šibenik and Rijeka. At the same time, for the first time it would enable the railway connection and financing of Istria County, Kvarner and Dalmatia with the rest of Croatia and with the European network,” said Brnjac, emphasising that the next step is a meeting with stakeholders from the governments of the countries through which the route would pass. The initiative will, she said, also influence the reconstruction of existing railway corridors as well as the construction of new lines. Tušek noted that without a modern railway there can be no strengthening of logistics capacities and position in the TEN-T network. He also highlighted the need to integrate the Istrian railways into the complete Croatian network, adding that study documentation for the Učka railway tunnel is currently being prepared. In this regard, he also announced that next year a tender will be issued for the Učka project, that is, the lowland railway project and the connection of Rijeka to that lowland railway.

financing the future adriatic-ionion corridor

Returning to the Adriatic-Ionian corridor, the question of its financing also needs to be raised. Brnjac said that 81 billion euros of EU money is currently available until the next financial framework, of which 35 billion for transport, 30 for energy and 17.5 for military mobility, and that is why this initiative was launched, working on opening the regulation of the Trans-European Transport Network.

“When the regulation tender is opened, then the Adriatic-Ionian corridor would become an integral corridor and then we can have funds for further financing,” she stressed, noting that the only known deadline is that a large conference on this topic will be organised in the European Parliament at the beginning of next year. More specifically speaking, the final conference is planned in Brussels, when the initiative will be handed over to European Commission Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism Apostolos Tzitzikostas, who, she said, has recognised the importance of this initiative.

All the signatories are aware of the importance of the said corridor for Croatia both in terms of connectivity and tourism, so HŽ Infrastruktura Management Board President Damir Lončarić emphasised that the Adriatic-Ionian railway corridor is a strategic issue for the state. “HŽ Infrastruktura is ready to make a full contribution in terms of expert and operational support for this project,” Lončarić added. The sheer importance of this massive project is further heightened by the security and geopolitical circumstances in Europe, as the war in Ukraine has shown how important alternative and reliable transport routes are for the economy, energy and military mobility. In addition, a more modern railway would enable faster freight transport, relieve road traffic and stronger inclusion of Croatian ports in the international chain.

World.title: Croatian Subjects Found to Have Forever Chemicals in Them Speak Out
World.content:
October the 3rd, 2026 – Croatian subjects found to have so-called forever chemicals in them have spoken out, with one man from Lika having been found with the highest levels of all.

Gospić lawyer Vjekoslav Bušić, better known to the public as one of the founders and prominent representatives of the Citizens’ Initiative “Gospić is Our Home”, revealed in a report by Slobodan Mufic for Index that he has the worst findings among the ten Croatian participants in the study on the presence of PFAS compounds in the blood, also known as “forever chemicals”.

“I spoke with the other participants in the study and it turned out that the highest values of the four long-chain PFAS were found in me, even though I’ve only been living in Gospić for the last three and a half years. Interestingly, my wife is clean as a whistle. Her findings are phenomenally low, and we have practically the same lifestyle habits and eat the same food,” said Bušić.

7 from gospić, one from pula and two from knin

The study was commissioned by the Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament. The biological analyses were carried out by the Institute for Occupational Medicine of the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, and the toxicological interpretation of the results was done by Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. In addition to the seven people from Gospić, two more from Knin and one person from Pula were tested.

A total of 110 people from Croatia, Italy, Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Spain, Denmark and Finland took part. Among the participants were also women of reproductive age, residents of areas near the chemical industry and trade union representatives, which shows that this is not a randomly selected representative sample of the European population.

All four analysed long-chain PFAS compounds (PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS and PFOS) were found in all 110 participants. However, in 27 of them, or 25 percent, the sum was above the health-based reference value set by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). Of the ten Croatian participants included in the study, six had a sum above the reference value – that is, 60 percent. The sum of the four long-chain PFAS compounds in the study was compared with the reference concentration of 6.9 nanograms per millilitre of blood. Exceeding that value does not mean that a person will develop a disease, nor does it constitute a diagnosis. It is a health-based reference value linked to EFSA’s assessment of long-term exposure to PFAS compounds and possible effects on the immune system.

Bušić emphasises that he has no reliable explanation for his findings: “It’s difficult for me to assess what the cause could be; I can only speculate. I thought it might be because in the last year and a half I have really often walked around the silos in the former PPK Velebit. Maybe the problem is inhaling those particles – I don’t know myself.”

how dangerous are these forever chemicals?

“On the other hand, toxicologists warn that heavy metals, which were also found in the illegally disposed hazardous waste in Gospić, are in the long term much more toxic and dangerous to human health than those ‘forever chemicals’. In any case, the findings are what they are, but one should not draw some final and alarming conclusions about carcinogenicity from them. It seems to me that all of this is still quite unresearched,” says Bušić, and adds:

“I still believe that I live in one of the cleanest and best-preserved areas in all of Europe. It’s important that it remains so and that the remediation of the waste in Gospić is carried out in the best possible way. And who knows, maybe I ‘picked up’ the PFAS while I was living in Zagreb.” The testing was carried out in the first days of July this year in Brussels. Bušić says that the people from Gospić received a link where they could apply online: “We didn’t even know how many people were participating in the study; in the end we realised that there were ten of us from Croatia. Apart from the seven of us from Gospić, the application of one person from Pula and two people from Knin, also members of an association, was accepted.”

The office of Croatian MEP from the Greens/EFA, Gordan Bosanac, organised the participation of ten Croatian volunteers and their trip to Belgium for blood sampling. In June, Bosanac described the project as a study of people deliberately selected from areas with possible increased exposure to PFAS, for example near landfills or industrial plants.

“Given our situation, this was a good signal that we should perhaps carry out some biomonitoring on a wider circle of people. Especially on those who live relatively close to the silos in Gospić or those who worked at the Rakitovac municipal landfill, where that hazardous waste was also brought. And it would be interesting to see the findings of the people who worked for Josip Šincek, who transported and unloaded that waste,” said Bušić.

Josip Šincek is a Varaždin entrepreneur and the main suspect in the USKOK investigation into illegal waste management; investigators suspect that through related companies he organised the import and transport of plastic, mixed and medical waste from Croatia and abroad. In Gospić, his company operated from 2021 in the former PPK Velebit complex in Bilajska Street, where tens of thousands of tonnes of illegally disposed and partly hazardous waste were later discovered.

World.title: Plenković: Without Government Measures, Inflation Would be 7%
World.content:
October the 3rd, 2026 – PM Andrej Plenković has stated that without government measures, inflation would currently be 7% in Croatia.

The Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) recently published that the year-on-year inflation rate measured by the consumer price index in September amounted to 4.7 percent, and 0.9 percent compared to August. Poslovni reports that it accelerated by 0.5 percentage points compared to August on an annual basis, and by 0.8 percent compared to July.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković warned on Friday after a meeting with Bavarian Prime Minister Markus Söder that without government measures inflation would have been 35 percent higher and would have stood at around seven percent, instead of the 4.7 percent that is the first estimate by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) for September, Hina reports.

The DZS earlier today published that the year-on-year inflation rate measured by the consumer price index in September amounted to 4.7 percent, and 0.9 percent compared to August. It accelerated by 0.5 percentage points compared to August on an annual basis, and by 0.8 percent compared to July. Energy prices had the greatest impact on the rise in inflation, rising by 20.5 percent year-on-year in September, while food, beverages and tobacco rose by only 0.2 percent, and non-food industrial products fell by 1.4 percent.

“What is good is that other segments are going downwards; there we have succeeded with measures in mitigating the growth. Without government measures, the overall inflation rate would have been 35 percent higher – it would have been around seven percent,” Plenković said in response to journalists’ questions.

He also recalled that prices of motor fuels are lower due to the government’s weekly interventions and stated that at the moment blue diesel is 10 cents cheaper, eurosuper 20 cents cheaper, and eurodiesel as much as 32 cents cheaper than the prices that would have been formed without government measures.

He added that there is still room to mitigate the rise in fuel prices through interventions, because Croatia is in good time asking the European Commission for permission to exceptionally lower excise duties even below the minimum threshold set by European regulations. A new government intervention is expected next Monday.

World.title: Croatian Banks Hold Serious Wealth, but Inflation is Eating it
World.content:
October the 2nd, 2026 – Croatian banks are holding some serious wealth, but inflation is continually eating it and reducing its purchasing power.

According to the Croatian National Bank (HNB), in June 2026, Croatian citizens held 33 billion euros in current and savings accounts, and an additional 10 billion euros in term deposits. Emilio Gucec reports for Poslovni that due to inflation, Croatians are losing around 430 euros of purchasing power per year on bank deposits, and the difference compared to investing after ten years can reach almost 10,000 euros per inhabitant.

This is a decline in purchasing power, not the disappearance of money from accounts: the nominal amount remains the same and, with interest, even grows slightly, but because of inflation less can be bought with it over time. Current and savings accounts in practice carry no interest, so with the latest published inflation of 4.2 % (August 2026) that part of the money loses value at the full rate of inflation. Shorter-term deposits currently yield 1.45 %, so the real loss on them is 2.75 % per year. According to a calculation by the investment platform Finax, this together means a loss of purchasing power of approximately 430 euros per year per inhabitant, or around 1.7 billion euros at the level of the entire country.

A similar picture was seen throughout 2025, when that loss amounted to around 360 euros per inhabitant, and it was particularly pronounced in 2022 and 2023, when inflation in Croatia reached 10.8 % and 8.4 % annually, which in just two years meant a real decline in the purchasing power of money in bank accounts of almost 20 %.

“Money held in current and savings accounts today practically carries no interest, so every month it quietly loses value at the full rate of inflation. When we translate that into figures, the average inhabitant of Croatia loses around 430 euros of purchasing power per year in this way, and at the level of the entire country it is almost 1.7 billion euros every year anew,” says Emilio Gučec, country manager of Finax for Croatia.

If the total of 43 billion euros that today lies in households’ current, savings and term accounts were invested in a globally diversified ETF portfolio with a historical average return of around 7 % per year, that amount could grow to around 84.6 billion euros in ten years. If everything remains as it is, the same amount in bank accounts would grow to only around 44.5 billion euros. The difference of almost 40 billion euros at the national level amounts to approximately 10,000 euros of lost potential value growth per inhabitant.

“A bank account provides many Croatians with a sense of security, but that same ‘security’ in the long term costs them the real value of their savings. The old saying goes: he who saves, has. But in today’s conditions, money that simply sits in a current or savings account without any interest quietly loses exactly what it was supposed to preserve, which is why it is suitable only for a short-term reserve, and not for the long-term building of assets. According to the HNB’s projection, according to which inflation should settle at around 2.8 % by 2028, such money could after about thirty years have less than half of its present purchasing power. With investing the exact opposite rule applies: compound interest works quietly, but from year to year more and more noticeably,” Gučec adds.

Inflation, he says, for years slowly and almost imperceptibly melts the savings deposited in banks, while compound interest in investing works in the completely opposite direction: it multiplies funds from year to year. And the longer the money remains invested, the stronger that effect is, while in a bank account time, on the contrary, works against it.

World.title: Croatian Subjects Have Been Tested for “Forever Chemicals”
World.content:
October the 2nd, 2026 – A group of Croatian subjects were tested for the presence of so-called “forever chemicals”, and they were unfortunately discovered, in levels that are much too high.

Of the ten Croatian participants included in a new European study, six had the sum of four long-chain PFAS compounds, also known as “forever chemicals”, above the health-based reference value set by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). Vedran Salvia reports for Index that a worrying seven of the participants were from Gospić, and five of them were above that threshold.

forever chemicals were discovered in all participants

The study covered 110 people from nine European Union countries. All four analysed long-chain PFAS compounds were found in every participant. However, in 27 of them, or 25 percent, their sum was above the EFSA reference value. The study was commissioned by the Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament, and the interpretation of the results was carried out by researchers from Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Additional data on the Croatian participants was obtained by Index from the Greens/EFA office in the European Parliament. Thus we learn that, in addition to the seven people from Gospić, two more from Knin and one person from Pula were tested.

what exactly were they tested for?

The long-chain PFAS compounds for which the participants were tested are PFOA, PFOS, PFNA and PFHxS. These are four “forever chemicals” that EFSA considers together, i.e. it adds up their concentrations into the value ΣEFSA-4. If that value is above 6.9 ng/mL, it is considered to exceed the health-based reference threshold of EFSA. This does not mean that a person above that threshold will develop health problems, but that it is a level above the one EFSA considers health-acceptable for long-term exposure.

The participants were also tested for five ultra-short-chain PFAS compounds (TFA, PFPrA, TFMS, PFEtS and PFPrS). In the results, TFA stands out, while the remaining four compounds were found in traces or were not detected at all and are not of greater significance for this study.

how dangerous is all of this?

“Forever chemicals” is the popular name for a large group of synthetic organic compounds that are extremely difficult to break down and therefore remain in the environment for a long time and can pose a significant danger to human health and environmental quality. People are exposed to PFAS compounds primarily through food and drinking water, and some types can also enter the body from the environment in which they accumulate for years.

We previously dealt with the topic of “forever chemicals” in the case of the illegal disposal of thousands of tonnes of waste in Lika, where PFAS were found in groundwater. At that time we spoke with Prof. Dr. Branimir K. Hackenberger from the Department of Biology at Josip Juraj Strossmayer University in Osijek. He explained that PFOS remains in the body for three to five years. Another of the more problematic PFAS compounds is PFOA. For that “forever chemical”, Hackenberger says that the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified it in 2023 among substances carcinogenic to humans, while PFOS was classified among possible carcinogens.

what is tfa?

TFA stands out in particular – an ultra-short-chain PFAS compound that was found in all participants in this study. TFA can accumulate in water resources and plants, including crops used for human nutrition. It accounted for as much as 81.4 percent of the total mass of the six detected PFAS compounds, and its concentrations were on average 4.6 times higher than the sum of the four long-chain PFAS. The authors also note that the median TFA levels measured in this study are the highest recorded so far in human serum. The study states that TFA is relatively quickly excreted from the body, with an estimated half-life of 16 to 60 hours. The authors therefore conclude that the measured levels “probably result from frequent exposure to significant amounts of TFA in everyday life.”

As for this European study, it is important to emphasise that the findings in the tested residents of Gospić are not linked to the local waste landfill. This is an independent study of PFAS exposure among citizens of several European countries.

the croatian results stand out

The Greens/EFA office notes that in the entire sample that threshold was exceeded by a quarter of the participants, while among the Croatian participants it was as many as 60 percent, or six out of ten. They also note that the Croatian participants stand out in that their median ΣEFSA-4 (the line in the middle of the blue box in the photo below) is among the highest among the countries covered, while the median TFA (the line in the middle of the green box) is among the lowest.

The study also showed some patterns related to PFAS levels. Among the most important factors were sex and age: men had a median ΣEFSA-4 of 7.3 ng/mL, compared to 3.7 ng/mL in women, and levels increased with age in men but not in women. Higher levels of long-chain PFAS were associated with more frequent consumption of meat and fish and seafood. The authors warn that the study is not representative and that the number of participants per country is too small for reliable comparisons. They estimate that to detect even moderate differences between countries, at least 20 to 30 participants per country would be needed.

“pfas compounds must be banned”

Gordan Bosanac, MEP from Možemo and member of the Greens/EFA group, told Index that they launched the testing campaign in order to identify the best-known PFAS compounds, but also those that chemical lobbies are trying to protect by claiming that they do not accumulate in our bodies.

“The result is a clear reality: forever chemicals are in our blood. We tested 110 people in nine European countries and in every single person we found TFA, the smallest and most persistent compound from the PFAS group, and this is a substance that the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) classifies as reproductively toxic. Subsequently, in the Croatians tested, very high levels of the four ‘classic’ long-chain PFAS compounds were also found. There is no alternative: PFAS compounds must be banned, and the gradual phasing out of their production and use must be systematically planned, supported and implemented. We can no longer wait, nor can we allow ourselves to continue being the ones who pay the price. The biggest polluters, primarily chemical companies, should bear the costs of cleaning up the pollution. If the Commission and the Member States vote against a PFAS ban, they will be directly responsible for crimes against the environment and public health,” he explained.

He adds that through the revision of the REACH chemicals regulation we must ban the placing of PFAS in new products and packaging.

“However, banning the creation of new PFAS is not enough. We must also change our attitude towards existing PFAS that is already in products on the market, that is already in our waste, that is already in the nature around us. As we know, these are forever chemicals and they will not disappear on their own. At the level of the entire EU, we need a strategy to combat PFAS waste – how we dispose of and treat that waste and how we ensure that it does not penetrate into nature and pollute our environment and community,” he adds.

“the ec is aware of the harmfulness of pfas”

“At our request, and following the case of 37 thousand tonnes of illegally imported and disposed international waste in Gospić, where analyses established the presence of PFAS compounds in wastewater, two weeks ago the European Parliament discussed the dangers of PFAS compounds to human health.

Colleagues across Europe recognised the danger of this situation and Commissioner Várhelyi emphasised that the Commission is aware of the harmfulness of PFAS and is ready to help Member States in the disposal of toxic waste and the fight against cross-border economic crime. I’d once again like to call on Commissioner Várhelyi, Commissioner Roswall, as well as Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to come forward as soon as possible with concrete proposals on how Member States can effectively dispose of waste contaminated with ‘forever chemicals’ and protect their citizens and nature,” he says.

World.title: Croatian Man Pushes Serbian Man into Sea, Hajduk Fans Pay Fine
World.content:
October the 2nd, 2026 – A Croatian man has pushed a Serbian man into the sea in Makarska for refusing to remove a Crvena Zvezda (Red Star) shirt, and Hajduk fans have paid his fine.

The Society of Friends of Hajduk Makarska announced via its official Facebook page that the full amount needed to cover the fine and court costs for their member has been successfully collected. Index reports that the Croatian man was fined after he pushed a man, a citizen of Serbia wearing a Red Star Belgrade (Crvena Zvezda) football club shirt, into the sea on the Makarska waterfront. In their post, the Makarska fan association stated that their member “enabled a certain tourist from abroad to swim.”

The incident received a legal epilogue at the misdemeanour court, where the 43-year-old attacker was given a fine (between 700 and 4,000 euros) for disturbing public order and peace, after which he was released. However, a subsequent police investigation led to an unusual turn of events in which the attacked man himself ended up behind bars.

By reviewing his social media profiles, police officers established that the mentioned Serb had, in earlier public posts, glorified the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić and also insulted Croatia and its citizens with derogatory content. Because of these offences, the attacked man was sentenced to 14 days in prison.

World.title: BioMania Zagreb Named Among the 10 Best Restaurants in the World
World.content:
October the 1st, 2026 – Tripadvisor, the world’s leading review platform for the hospitality and tourism sector, has ranked BioMania Zagreb, a 100% plant-based and organic restaurant, among the top 10 in the world in the Vegan & Vegetarian category.

Less than two years after opening, BioMania Bistro Zagreb has entered the Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Best of the Best category for 2026. Fewer than 1% of all restaurants registered on the platform – and there are more than 5 million of them – make it into this category. Best of the Best is not awarded by a jury. The ranking is calculated based on the number and quality of reviews from guests who actually dined at the restaurant, backed by an editorial review process that places the winners among the top one percent on the platform.

Alongside BioMania, the world’s top 10 in the Vegan & Vegetarian category include restaurants from Peru, Greece, Vietnam, Canada, Scotland, the United States and the Czech Republic. The Zagreb restaurant is rated 4.9 out of 5 on Tripadvisor, based on more than a thousand reviews.

“We are truly overjoyed that, after our seasonal bistro in Bol, our year-round Zagreb restaurant has also received this prestigious award and been ranked among the top 1% of restaurants in the world. Being among the top 10 in the world in our category is truly a dream come true. I would like to sincerely thank our entire team and all our wonderful partners, especially the many small producers of organic and biodynamic fruit, vegetables and herbs. Finally, of course, I would also like to thank our many guests, who show their appreciation by leaving reviews, coming back in great numbers and telling their friends, acquaintances and relatives about us. In this way they help our guest numbers grow steadily, which is also helped by the fact that the vast majority of our menu is gluten-free. In just under two years since opening, we have welcomed more than 40,000 guests, and we are especially pleased that over 70% of them are from Croatia.

“We were also surprised that more than 80% of our guests are ‘omnivores’, which further shows us that, both conceptually and gastronomically, we have succeeded in attracting a very broad range of guests,” said Dario Kožul, founder of the BioMania brand.
