World.title: Meghan book ‘signed to Princess Eugenie’ listed on eBay
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Meghan book ‘signed to Princess Eugenie’ listed on eBay Victoria Ward October 3, 2026 — 12:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A signed copy of the Duchess of Sussex’s children’s book, inscribed to Princess Eugenie, has appeared for sale on eBay. The hardback copy of The Bench, listed for sale for £20,000 ($38,000), features a handwritten note seemingly in Meghan’s hand, dated 2021 – two years after the birth of her son, Archie. The seller of the book claimed the inscription was “written in the Duchess’s highly celebrated, fluid signature calligraphy style”. It was listed by Drive Easy’s Signed Books, owned by Nicholas Joseph Greenwood, a specialist bookseller, who has sold more than 2000 items and has a 100 per cent positive feedback rating. The inscription reads: “Dear Eug & Jack, Celebrating the special bond between father and son. I wrote this poem at Frogmore – I hope that Eug, you witness the same love there with your guys. All love, Meghan.”



Princess Eugenie and Jack Brooksbank, her husband, temporarily moved into Frogmore Cottage in Windsor after Meghan and Harry relocated to the US. Their elder son, August, was born in February 2021. The listing had attracted more than 20,000 views by Friday (UK time), before it was either sold or withdrawn from sale. Harry and Meghan in Melbourne during their visit to Australia in April. Getty Images A spokesman for Meghan declined to comment on the sale or the book’s authenticity. The listing on eBay noted that the ink from the inscription had “gone through to the previous page” but described it as “an absolute masterpiece of modern royal history”.



It added: “Written in the Duchess’s highly celebrated, fluid signature calligraphy style, the personal message links the Sussexes directly to the heart of the British Royal family. “Authentic intimate gifts sent from one member of the Royal family directly to another are exceptionally rare to find on the open market. This book is thus a pinnacle piece for any serious royal memorabilia collector, autograph hunter, or contemporary archivist.” Jack Brooksbank and Princess Eugenie at Ascot Racecourse in 2025. Getty Images Princess Eugenie, who is Prince Harry’s cousin, is one of the few members of the Royal family known to have stayed close to the Sussexes since they stepped away from public duties. The two couples are now neighbours, each owning beachfront properties in Portugal. Harry and Meghan Markle, his then girlfriend, were with Princess Eugenie and her husband-to-be in Toronto when the news of their relationship became public knowledge in October 2016.



The four dressed up for Halloween to enjoy “one final fun night out” before their relationship was revealed to the world. In February 2022, Harry was joined by Princess Eugenie at the Super Bowl in California. She was the only member of the Royal family to appear in new footage in the duke and duchess’s Netflix documentary, released in Dec 2022, after visiting the couple in Montecito, California. Greenwood did not respond to a query about how or where he had sourced the book. Telegraph, London Read more royal news:

World.title: Former Kangaroos star Dane Gagai makes shock Kiwis switch
World.content:
Dane Gagai will make a shock switch of allegiance to New Zealand for the Rugby League World Cup, eight years after he last represented Australia. Gagai, who is hoping for a fairytale farewell from Newcastle with a grand final victory before switching to Brisbane, will join teammate Kayln Ponga in the Kiwis squad. Gagai’s application to change his allegiance was initially knocked back, given players aren’t allowed to switch between tier-one nations Australia, England and New Zealand. Dane Gagai will play for Kangaroos. Getty However, an IRL appeals committee ultimately ruled that the veteran centre wasn’t afforded a chance to benefit from a rule tweak that has allowed other players to switch their allegiance. The IRL recently permitted Ponga to switch to New Zealand and AJ Brimson to play for England after both had represented Australia at the IRL World Cup Nines in 2019. Changes to State of Origin eligibility rules also enabled Briton Nikora, Casey McLean and Addin Fonua-Blake to play in this year’s Origin series despite not being eligible for Australia as they have represented New Zealand.



IRL chair Troy Grant said there were “special circumstances” in the case of Gagai, who hasn’t represented the Kangaroos since 2018. He added that ARLC executive chairman Peter V’landys and Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters supported Gagai’s application. “Dane hasn’t played for Australia for eight years and we didn’t want him to be disadvantaged compared to other players with recent rule changes,” Grant said. “Dane wrote to us and Peter V’landys was very supportive. He felt there should be a bit of an amnesty period because we didn’t want one player disadvantaged over another, given that Dane wasn’t in the Kangaroos squad and it has been so long since he has played at international level. Kevin Walters was supportive too. “Dane didn’t have the same option as other players who can play State of Origin and represent their heritage. “It was felt that there were special circumstances in his case so Dane is now available for selection by New Zealand, and it is now up to them whether they pick him.”



Grand final dreamtime: How Knights’ Indigenous stars will break new ground on Sunday Christian Nicolussi Newcastle will head into Sunday’s NRL decider with the highest representation of Indigenous players ever in a grand final team. The only shame is that the five Knights Indigenous representatives – Bradman Best, Dane Gagai, Dylan Lucas, Jermaine McEwen and Fletcher Hunt – will be forced to miss the Koori Knockout, the popular Indigenous tournament being played in their own backyard over the long weekend. Koori Knights players Fletcher Hunt, Dylan Lucas, Jermaine McEwen, Bradman Best and Dane Gagai. Marija Ercegovac/SMH



In an illustration of how much the Koori Knockout means to the Indigenous community, McEwen joked that his family and friends were still undecided about whether to stay back to watch the annual tournament, where his younger brother Matthew will represent hometown heroes the Newcastle Yowies, or head to Sydney to watch him play against the Roosters at Accor Stadium. Cronulla had Indigenous quartet Jack Bird, Andrew Fifita, Ben Barba and Wade Graham feature in their 2016 premiership win over Melbourne, but never has a grand final team featured five First Nations players, according to statistician David Middleton. Middleton added that Gagai, who now sits on 339 career games, had quietly slipped past Cliff Lyons (332) earlier this year to become the most capped Indigenous player in premiership history. Best first represented Tingha in 2023, then switched to the Yowies, who are shooting for successive victories. McEwen, whose father, Matt, is of Aboriginal descent – and whose mob is from Gulargambone, in the state’s central west – has regularly represented the Yowies. Loading



Just as they were inspired watching North Queensland speedster Matt Bowen, Johnathan Thurston and South Sydney’s Greg Inglis, the Newcastle quintet knew they were responsible for encouraging the next generation of Indigenous stars. “The knockout does so much for the region, it brings the mob and family together, and to miss it is a little bittersweet – but obviously playing in an NRL grand final is where you want to be,” Best said. “Koori fellas that come from remote areas, and might not have much, if we can put them on the right path … league is the greatest game, it brings everyone together, young Koori kids aspire to be NRL players, and it’s special knowing what kind of impact we can have on them.” Gagai, 35, who represented the Yowies more than a decade ago, alongside former Knights centre Timana Tahu, said being Indigenous role model was something he took seriously. Nicho Hynes and Andrew Fifita turned out for Griffith Three Ways United at the Koori Knockout in 2019. Dominic Lorrimer



“I was a kid once upon a time, I loved watching Matty Bowen, and now we get to have the same impact on community,” he said. “There are a lot of Indigenous players in the NRL doing unbelievable things, none more so than Latrell Mitchell. I guarantee you there isn’t one teammate who has not loved playing with him. Away from the field, he’s a family man, a proud Indigenous man who does so many good things for Indigenous kids. “The impact we can have on Indigenous kids, whether they want to play footy or not, it’s about being a good person … if we can encourage and help them in any way, it’s the best feeling.” Lucas was ready to represent Nanima Common Connection this weekend if there were no issues with his ankle. “It’s a massive weekend,” Lucas said. “Our people come together, kids meet their idols and rub shoulders with NRL players – it fills my cup and I get to play footy with the brothers I don’t play with … except for this weekend.”



How Roosters skipper bounced back after Blues snub Adrian Proszenko When James Tedesco was dropped from the NSW side for the start of the 2024 series, it was meant to signal the beginning of the end. After a storied run of form that had earned him a Dally M Medal, two RLPA players’ champion awards, three Brad Fittler Medals and a Wally Lewis Medal, some critics felt there was only one way to go after being sacked as state skipper.



Loading Yet, it could be argued that the form the Roosters star has produced since, culminating in another grand final appearance on Sunday against Newcastle, has been every bit as spectacular as anything he has produced during his storied career. A second Dally M Medal last year, the reclaiming of his Blues jersey and a potential World Cup berth with the Kangaroos is proof that, at the age of 33, “Teddy” is far from done. “That’s always motivation for me when people doubt or criticise me,” Tedesco said. “I’ve grown up with that and had a lot of it throughout my career, even in the early days when people told me I wasn’t good enough or wasn’t going to make it. That sort of drove me.



James Tedesco has a laugh at training this week as he prepares for his third grand final. Getty Images “I always had belief and confidence in my footy. When I’m not the best player on the field, that’s when the critics come out. It’s a pretty high bar, but I understand that. “For me now, I don’t have to be the best player on the field; I just have to be a great leader and do my job. I have so much confidence and belief in the team we have. I feel very lucky to captain this team. I just have to do my job on Sunday, let these boys play, and that excites me as a leader.” One of the criticisms of Tedesco, around the time he was dropped by the Blues, was that he was trying to do too much himself. The former Tiger admits there have been times when he overplayed his hand in the belief it was his responsibility to lead teams to victory. However, he has worked out that sometimes less is more.



James Tedesco celebrates his match-winning try for NSW in Origin I in 2026. NRL Photos “I’ve gone through that battle,” he said. “It’s always a balance for me – whether it’s around the middle or on the edges – finding that line between doing too much and staying involved. “I’m always going to be in the game, that’s just how I play. Throughout my career, I’ve sometimes gotten caught in trying to do too much and get my hands on the ball. Those are important lessons to learn. I don’t like when I overplay; I just want to be involved, so it’s about finding that balance. “Nothing really changed in terms of how I play the game. I always just try to work harder on all my skills and then play without overthinking too much. Overthinking is what causes bad performances.” Given the talent-laden Roosters side – 11 players have played at State of Origin level – coach Trent Robinson reminded Tedesco he doesn’t need to overburden himself.



Related Article NRL 2026 Knights attracted more fans to a training session than some actual game days “I’ll always come up with plays when I need to and be in the game, but I don’t need to go over-searching for it,” Tedesco said. The mental side of the game is just as important for Tedesco as the physical. He has long leant on mindset mentor Joe Wehbe to focus on the things that matter. “I’ve always got communication with Joe every week,” he said. “That hasn’t changed throughout my career, whether I’m playing really well or not as well. “It’s funny – your mind can be so powerful, but it can also be detrimental in the way you think about the game and yourself. The constant communication with Joe helps me stay clear in my mind and keep that confidence and belief in myself. His leadership and steering me in the right direction have always been really important.”



Harrison Graham has started in four NRL games. On Sunday, he starts in a grand final Adrian Proszenko Newcastle hooker Harrison Graham is adamant he is ready to fill the void left by suspended teammate Phoenix Crossland in Sunday’s grand final despite wearing the starting No.9 jersey just four times in his NRL career. Crossland described the fallout from a tackle that broke the leg of Nathan Cleary as “the worst couple of days of my life” after copping a four-game suspension. The New Zealand international will miss the decider against the Roosters and the start of the Kiwis’ World Cup campaign after his sanction was handed down on Tuesday night. Graham has been a capable foil for Crossland via the interchange bench, but has started only twice for the Knights since switching from the Dolphins at the end of last season.



The Knights have named uncapped rookie Diesel Hagan in their extended squad, raising the prospect of him becoming the first player to debut in a grand final since Eddie Lockhart for Balmain against the Roosters in 1936. Newcastle’s Harrison Graham will have to step up and fill the void left by a suspended Phoenix Crossland. Sitthixay Ditthavong Regardless, Graham believes he is ready for whatever Newcastle requires from him on Sunday. “I’m ready for whatever the team needs me for,” Graham said. “A few weeks back in New Zealand, before the finals, I started over there against a quality outfit. Going into that week, I knew I had to stand up because Phoenix was out, and I just tried to bring what he brings to the team … I’ll just have to do that again.”



Crossland won the Danny Buderus medal as Newcastle’s best player of the season, and both men have had a huge influence on Harrison. “He’s been massive,” Graham said of Crossland. “We’re best mates on and off the field. He epitomises what a Newcastle Knights player is, and everyone looks up to him. “He’s been our best player all year. His effort areas are the big thing for him, including a lot of things people probably don’t see or that don’t get recognised enough. That’s how he’s helped me.” Knights legend Buderus, now a member of Justin Holbrook’s coaching staff, has been a mentor to Graham.



Related Article NRL 2026 ‘Shouldn’t be mentioned in the same sentence’: Knights No.7 feeling weight of Joey’s jersey “Oh mate, he’s awesome,” Graham said of Buderus. “Since I came here last November, I’ve just been trying to pick his brain every week. We sit down and watch a lot of video together. “He was arguably the best player in his position, and he’s awesome to learn from. “I just try to keep picking his brain, even when I’m out on the field and he runs out to give us water. I’m always bouncing ideas off him, he’s been massive for me.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: This play is set in the past but raises questions about AI that are more prescient than ever
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Eliza at Southbank Theatre is a psychological thriller

THEATRE: Koreaboo at Malthouse draws from lived experience

OPERA: Victorian Opera take on Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of The Screw

MUSIC: Lady Blackbird performs at Melbourne Recital Centre

THEATRE

Eliza ★★★★★

Southbank Theatre, The Sumner until October 31 Prognoses of AI’s impact upon humanity has reached fever pitch, but in Tom Holloway’s play, we are catapulted into the past to grapple with the very same questions we’re seeking answers to 60 years later. Dan Spielman (left) and Manali Datar in Eliza. Pia Johnson Dr Joseph Weizenbaum (Dan Spielman) is a mercurial visiting professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as intent on repressing the traumatic memories of his escape from Nazi Germany as he is on heralding the advent of digital computers. When his secretary, Becky (a bewitching Manali Datar) makes a seemingly inconsequential joke about the back-and-forth cadence of talk therapy, it opens the doors to the creation of the world’s first chatbot: Eliza. The breathtaking scale of invention is mirrored in the expansiveness of Dale Ferguson’s vertiginous set. Rows upon rows of systematically aligned towers of working files and cascading sheets of glass lend an unexplainable depth and dimension to the stage, creating rabbit warrens for the characters to lose themselves in as their sense of reality and personhood begin to blur.



The play traces the ethical quandaries inherent in AI back to its genesis. Weizenbaum is shown to be well-meaning, but his disavowal of personal disclosure, refusal to listen until it’s too late and his betrayal of Becky, in particular, is a recurring theme that can be extrapolated to AI’s routine, large-scale copyright thefts in the present day. The famed sycophancy of AI that is leading to current crises of consciousness is shown to have had very much the same effect when it was conceived in the 1960s, as people yearned to unburden themselves to what they perceived to be a neutral entity. Although set in the 1960s, Eliza raises philosophical and ethical concerns about the role of AI in society. Pia Johnson Under Paige Rattray’s direction, the rapid-fire play unfurls at the brisk pace of a psychological thriller as a collective psychosis and breakdown of legibility takes hold of the characters in different ways, as they around one another without truly understanding each other. This strange incomprehension finds its expression in the motif of starlings, which is, incidentally, the namesake of a company spying on Weizenbaum’s exploits. Through spectacular audiovisual mastery and a stunning Hitchcockian reckoning, the forward march of progress is disturbingly realised in increasingly absurd and surreal ways as Weizenbaum figuratively and literally chokes on the irreversible weight of what he has set in motion.



Spielman excels as the fulcrum, superbly marrying the constant whirring of a beautiful mind with an inexplicable childlike naivete. Datar’s transition from unknowing to seemingly all-knowing in a role that Holloway resurrected from the annals of history is chilling, and there isn’t a role that Hamish Michael can’t play, as he dovetails seamlessly between aggrieved research assistant, enthused journalist and lofty powers that be. The philosophical and ethical concerns that Eliza raises are by no means new to anyone engaged in the broader debate around AI, but in this undidactic, morally nuanced play, the inextricability of latent humanity and technological advancement is laid bare once more.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair THEATRE

Koreaboo ★★★

Malthouse, until October 10 Inspired by playwright Michelle Lim Davidson’s own experiences and directed by Jessica Arthur, Koreaboo is a two-hander that surveys contentious issues of race, diaspora and belonging, with a light touch. Heather Jeong (left) and Michelle Lim Davidson in a scene from Koreaboo. Gianna Rizzo



Davidson herself plays Hannah, a young Australian who travels to Seoul in an attempt to reconnect with her estranged birth mother, Umma (Heather Jeong). It’s only their second meeting. We learn that although she was born in South Korea, Hannah was adopted as a baby and grew up in Newcastle, NSW. At the start, the two women fail and flail in communication. Hannah was expecting a summer-long stay – a long enough period, perhaps, for meaningful reconnection; Umma (mother in Korean), however, believed it was just going to be a short vacation. The two women in Koreaboo fail and flail in communication. Gianna Rizzo Umma’s behaviour toward her daughter thrums with wariness, as though one were greeting a stranger. Maybe, she suggests, Hannah should be visiting Seoul’s touristy spots instead. The entire performance is staged in a small convenience store run by Umma, lovingly decked out in all manner of brightly coloured snacks, and with harsh fluorescent lighting thanks to designer Mel Page. The two women move within the space as they interrogate, parry and deflect.



Davidson explores a raft of issues, including the question of identity. Hannah’s hyphenated background (Korean-Australian) means she’s part of both cultures and wholly of neither, and at first, Umma’s brusque criticism of Hannah’s language skills feels like a wholesale rejection of her daughter’s “Koreanness”. Seeking both maternal and cultural acceptance, Hannah feels crushed to receive neither. Related Article Performing arts Star of ABC hit The Newsreader mines real-life family drama for new project Their common language – and one that helps them move toward connection and bridge distance, it turns out – is K-pop. The title actually refers to someone who’s not of Korean heritage but who is obsessed with Korean pop culture. Koreaboo swerves to the unexpected and surreal when both performers begin to sing and dance. There is a talent show in the offing to prepare for, and a chance for Hannah to become more Korean. It’s all surface-level cultural appropriation, though, much in the same way that Umma learnt English by watching TV, becoming so familiar with the lives of the characters in Sex and the City that she can quote from them. After a shaky start, Jeong and Davidson become good sparring partners and friends as they navigate the tricky mother-daughter relationship anew after years apart. Umma’s backstory is revealed: the reasons behind Hannah’s adoption and how her yearnings for a singing career were quashed because of filial obedience to her own mother. Korean culture is not just skincare and pop music, but, like a lot of Asian countries, there’s an expectation to conform to parental demands.



Koreaboo packs in a lot during its 90-minute stage time – maybe too much, as there is a lot of jumping about trying to cover a lot of ground. The beginning set-up takes a while to develop and can be tightened, and the ending feels rushed. And although the singing and dance sequences are overextended and as distracting as they are humorous, the play’s value is drawn from highlighting the possible consequences of adopting a child, removing them from their motherland, and raising them in an entirely foreign environment. Even if they embrace the riches of a new life in their host country, there are always losses to be reckoned with.

Reviewed by Thuy On OPERA

The Turn of the Screw ★★★

Palais Theatre, until October 1 Operatic takes on the supernatural span the centuries, but no modern work is more revered and feared than Benjamin Britten’s The Turn of the Screw. The 1954 opera follows a governess who takes up residence at an English country house, only to find the spirits of two dead servants are haunting the children now in her care. From left: Rachelle Durkin, Genevieve Gray and Oliver Thadoe Naing in The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby



Finally, an opera where the muffled screams drifting in from Luna Park next door actually add to the drama, rather than detract! This is a piece that has potential to be The Shining-level unnerving. When staged up close and creepy, the eerie singing and sinister spectacle can captivate like a demonic spirit itself. Here, the huge set and vast stage dwarf the drama – in pivotal moments, the singers are far away from each other; we are far away from them. Detachment creates a disconnect that does not serve some excellent performances. Durkin, Michaela Cadwgan and Kanen Breen in The Turn of the Screw. Jeff Busby It is, after all, a chamber opera. Britten scored it for just 13 instruments. Perhaps no Australian conductor knows more about the English composer than Paul Kildea, and the reduced Orchestra Victoria was guided superbly by him. Rachelle Durkin (Governess) was more maternal than hysterical, with a self-assured, impressive vocal performance to match. Kanen Breen’s voice is sharp and cold and uses his lithe physicality to intensify Peter Quint’s menace, despite donning the most unflattering wig anyone’s ever been cursed to wear (it’s a confusing choice, when it’s clearly mentioned how handsome Quint is).



One exceptional discovery to come from this production is soprano Genevieve Gray (currently a university student), who sings the older child, Flora. Gray possesses a vocal evenness and an array of colour that belies her youth. Neither a spook nor a snore, though with moments of satisfaction, this production feels like a missed opportunity to bewitch more people with the mystery and magic of operatic storytelling.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies MUSIC

Lady Blackbird ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, September 30 It’s been decades since Lady Blackbird – raised in an evangelical Christian household in New Mexico – abandoned her church-music roots, along with the religious doctrines that no longer defined her. Singer Lady Blackbird.



These days, the message underpinning her music is much more personal, but no less spiritually charged. The American singer (born Marley Munroe) has a voice to rival any gospel queen, but it’s now self-empowerment and self-acceptance she champions, rather than submission to an external force. In Melbourne on Wednesday, as part of her debut Australian tour, Lady Blackbird cut a striking figure as she arrived on stage: floor-sweeping black dress, elegant cane and signature platinum afro. Her three-piece band (guitarist Chris Seefried, bassist Jonathan Flaugher and Melbourne drummer Felix Bloxsom) stoked a gritty, distortion-flecked fire around the singer for Pink Floyd’s Mother, then retreated to the shadows for Blackbird, the haunting Nina Simone song that inspired the singer’s stage moniker. Related Article Melbourne live reviews Just the right amount of silly: Spamalot comes back to Melbourne On Collage, the amped-up fuzz of electric bass and guitar magnified the drama but almost submerged Blackbird’s glorious vocals. Then the mood softened – first with the addition of acoustic bass, then acoustic guitar. This was Blackbird in heartfelt confessional mode, her gorgeously grainy voice brimming with emotion on a clutch of originals: the soulfully swaying Lost and Looking, the jazz-tinted Five Feet Tall and the lilting, folky Man on a Boat. Seefried switched to piano for the wistful If I Told You before ushering in another cloud of psychedelia on a heady rendition of The Beatles’ Come Together. Blackbird’s musical world is unconstrained by genre, and her emotional commitment and authenticity allow her to make each song her own, whether it was written by her or others.



Imaginative arrangements and reharmonisations also allow the audience to hear old songs with fresh ears. In Blackbird’s hands, Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door became a hushed torch song, exquisitely understated. Her spellbinding encore – I Am What I Am – was equally unadorned, stripped of its Broadway sequins to become a quietly defiant affirmation of identity.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Multiple people injured after car crashes into Newcastle Knights fans
World.content:
Nine people are in hospital, two in critical condition, after a driver crashed into a crowd of Newcastle Knights fans, shocking locals who were lining the roads for kilometres to send off the home team ahead of tomorrow’s grand final against the Sydney Roosters. NSW Ambulance said of the nine injured, one was in critical condition, one was critical but stable, and the remaining injured were in a stable condition. The crash scene. TNV Police do not believe the incident was targeted, and are investigating if the driver lost control of his vehicle in the moments before the collision. The driver of the vehicle was arrested by NSW Police.



Newcastle Mayor Gavin Morris said children were among those injured, though NSW Ambulance would not confirm the ages of those injured. “It’s just been a magical week of positivity and support, and we’ve all come together,” he said. “So it was an absolute shock to hear the news this morning, and yeah, the information has been coming through, you know, over the last 30, 40 minutes now, so it’s really upsetting,” Morris told ABC television just a short time ago. Loading Earlier reports suggested children had been among those injured, but the NSW Ambulance media spokesperson wouldn’t comment other than to say injured were of varying ages.



NSW Police said a large emergency services response was underway, and said the driver was arrested at the scene. Emergency services were called to Newcastle Link Road at the Transfield Drive roundabout in Wallsend at about 9.30am following reports a vehicle had struck multiple people as the crowd gathered to support the Knights ahead of the grand final with the Roosters on Sunday. Police said several people had been injured and were receiving treatment at the scene. Others have been transported to John Hunter Hospital in Newcastle. Scenes at Wallsend, Newcastle, after a car crashed into a crowd of Knights supporters. The incident has impacted the planned route of the Newcastle Knights grand final procession, which has been diverted to an alternate route.



Sonia Hornery, NSW MP for Wallsend, posted that she’d just become aware of an incident involving a vehicle colliding with pedestrians while Knights fans were there to cheer on the team coach. “Emergency services are on site. Newcastle Link Road is closed in both directions. Please avoid the area. I hope everyone involved is ok,” she said. Newcastle Knights said because of the incident, the team bus heading to Sydney for the grand final had been diverted. Paramedics prepare to transport the injured by helicopter. Sitthixay Ditthavong “We apologise to anyone who was waiting and missed the boys, but public safety is our priority,” the announcement said.



This masthead’s chief sports reporter Tom Decent, who was interviewing fans when the incident happened, said word started coming through that many people had been hit by a car and were severely injured. “There are thousands and thousands of Knights fans on the street waiting to watch their heroes come through on the team but, but that’s now not happening,” Decent said. “That excitement has turned to confusion and concern for their fellow fans. It’s chaos here at the moment. People have realised something very serious has happened.” The Premier Chris Minns said it was heartbreaking to see fans who were sending off their grand final team involved in such a terrible incident.



“My thoughts are with the families and friends of loved ones who have been involved or injured in the crash. I also want to thank emergency services including police and ambulance who are responding to this tragedy”, the premier said. “We’ve seen how this grand final has brought the Newcastle together, and I hope the whole community remains united as we continue to respond.” Locals reported on social media that they were stuck in traffic on the Link Road, reporting multiple helicopters overhead, and more than 30 emergency responders. Newcastle Link Road is closed in both directions and is expected to remain closed for some time while inquiries continue. Newcastle Knights fans gathered to send off their team. Nine



The team bus had now departed Newcastle. Police said they acknowledged many loyal supporters may have missed the opportunity to see the team and show their support. Members of the public were asked to leave the area and keep roadways clear to assist emergency services and traffic management efforts. Officers attached to Newcastle City Police District are on scene, assisted by Traffic and Highway Patrol Command officers and NSW Ambulance paramedics. Newcastle residents said helicopters were whirring overhead, and the incident had blocked the Newcastle Link Road, the major route to Sydney. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Christa Pike ‘on a ventilator and unconscious’ after failed execution
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty Christa Pike ‘on a ventilator and unconscious’ after failed execution Kim Chandler and James Stengle Updated October 3, 2026 — 11:13am ,first published October 3, 2026 — 5:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content Convicted killer Christa Pike was placed on a ventilator and unconscious in a hospital in the hours after her failed execution in Tennessee, her lawyers said in a court filing. Hospital staff, her lawyers said, were working to save Pike’s life and clear two doses of the drug that the states uses to execute prisoners. Loading The stunning failure in Tennessee’s execution chamber on Wednesday has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review.



The court filing on Friday (US time) offered the first detailed account of Pike’s condition after an ambulance took her from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Her attorneys said on Thursday she was in critical condition. Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream. Christa Pike cries in 1996 after being sentenced to death. WBIR-TV via AP “Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” they wrote. Instead of “remedying this failure”, they prepared and administered a back-up set of pentobarbital syringe, her lawyers said.



State officials have not offered any explanations about what went wrong. Related Article Graphic content

Death penalty How Christa Pike’s botched Tennessee execution unfolded, minute by minute Lee demanded a review of the execution procedures and indefinitely postponed Pike’s execution and another scheduled for this year. Republican Tennessee lawmakers said the state should review whether to stop single-drug lethal injections and consider other options to carry out death sentences. There are also new doubts about whether any future attempt to execute Pike can ever proceed. The New York Times reported that Pike’s present condition sets the stage for an unprecedented ethical and legal quagmire, with any future attempt relying on whether she is deemed capable of what the Supreme Court has described as a “rational understanding” of why she is to be put to death.



The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Pike’s defence lawyer Randy Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm. Neither the initial nor the back-up dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike, 50, was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has postponed Payne’s execution and ordered a review of the week’s incident. AP Pike’s attorneys asked a state court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve all evidence from the failed execution. “Preserving this evidence is essential to understanding what happened, ensuring accountability and protecting Christa’s legal rights,” two of her attorneys said in a statement.



Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, 19, in a jealous rage. She later became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Following the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, her attorneys said. Photographs of Colleen Slemmer, who was murdered in 1995, outside Riverbend Maximum Security Institution this week. AP “It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in an earlier clemency petition. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, expressed frustration over the failed execution. “I didn’t get justice for my daughter,” Martinez said on Thursday.



Four years ago, Tennessee’s governor ordered another independent review into capital punishment after abruptly stopping the April 2022 execution of Oscar Smith. Lee then paused all executions after acknowledging the state had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were properly tested. Months later, a report found the state hadn’t complied with its own lethal injection process since its revision in 2018, which resulted in executions being conducted without drugs being properly tested. May Martinez (left), the mother of murder victim Colleen Slemmer, on Wednesday. AP At the time, the state used a three-drug execution protocol of midazolam, vecuronium bromide and potassium chloride. The state later switched to using just pentobarbital. Pentobarbital has been used to carry out death sentences in multiple states and by the federal government.



The previous review in Tennessee, led by former US attorney Ed Stanton, also found that the state’s unidentified executioner had no formal healthcare training and learnt the role mainly through on-the-job experience. After the release of the report, the Tennessee Department of Correction fired its longtime top attorney and another employee. World.title: ‘Absolute devastation’ for Watson, but Roosters don’t want week off before grand finals
World.content:
Roosters coach Trent Robinson maintains there is no need for the NRL to schedule a week off before the grand final despite the “absolute devastation” Connor Watson is experiencing after being the first player to miss a decider due to the 11-day concussion protocols. Watson has been ruled out of Sunday’s clash against Newcastle – which would have doubled as his farewell Roosters game before joining the Dragons for next season – after suffering a concussion against the Dolphins in the preliminary final. Connor Watson at the Roosters’ captain’s run on Saturday morning. Getty Images After initially displaying category-two symptoms, the representative utility was upgraded to a category one. It meant Watson would be unable to play or train for 11 days under the NRL’s concussion protocols, effectively ruling him out of the grand final. There is a provision under the rules that allowed the Roosters to seek a reclassification or exemption based on independent medical advice, although the club ultimately opted not to do so.



It has raised debate over whether the NRL should give the grand final teams a week off to avoid the situation that has ultimately ended Watson’s dream of a fairytale club farewell. But while Robinson felt for his star utility, he wasn’t in favour of any change. “Look, I think these are unfortunate things that happen, but we have protocols for a reason,” Robinson said. Loading “I’m more for the week off before the finals than I am before the grand final. I feel like momentum is built throughout the finals series, and the attrition part of it is a part of our game, so I understand that.” Robinson had no issue with the protocols that resulted in Watson’s scratching, given they were implemented to protect the health of the players. The three-time premiership-winning coach added that Watson had taken the news “stoically”.



“It’s probably who Connor is,” Robinson said. “Connor’s a good man, a strong man, he’s his own man, and so he had to control all of that. He knew we were in the middle of a [training] session. The absolute devastation that it is for him and all the work that’s gone into his football career for him, his family, and friends, and then you get news like that – it’s quite tough. “But then he spoke to the group quite clearly about how this is about the group, and he passed that on … Trent Robinson and Mark Nawaqanitawase at the Roosters’ captain’s run. Getty Images “You can have all the pain in the world, and in the present moment, that’s a lot of pain for him. But he also knows who he is, what he’s done, his role in this team, and what he wants from this team. Someone as stoic as Connor is going to hold that emotion, give positive energy to the crew, and move on. That’s exactly what he did.” The Roosters will go into the grand final as overwhelming favourites, but Newcastle believes it has one more major upset in them. Knights coach Justin Holbrook – who has twice worked as an assistant to Robinson – dismissed suggestions his team had played their grand final early, in last weekend’s epic win over Penrith.



Related Article NRL 2026 The Cessnock Curtain: How Fletcher Sharpe – and his hair – became the face of Newcastle “My response to [the critics] is that last week was a prelim, it wasn’t a grand final. We know that,” Holbrook said. “Someone said it the week before after the Warriors game, that it was our grand final, but we knew it wasn’t. We know the grand final is tomorrow, so we’re not silly. “I can understand it because we’ve got on a roll and gone up the ladder over recent weeks if you want to look at it that way. But that’s irrelevant now. We’re so happy and excited to come to training and play, so we get another chance to do that tomorrow. We understand tomorrow is the grand final, and we’ve always known that.”

World.title: Flydubai attack suspect was banned from flying by Oman over extremism concerns
World.content:
Updated WorldMiddle EastAviation Flydubai attack suspect was banned from flying by Oman over extremism concerns Sheikh Saaliq Updated October 3, 2026 — 12:54pm ,first published October 2, 2026 — 6:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The co-pilot who allegedly stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight had been banned from flying by Oman, according to US media reports. The Wall Street Journal, CNN and the Associated Press have reported that the co-pilot was removed from an Omani airline last year over concerns about his radical views, with the outlets citing sources familiar with the matter. Loading Despite the ban, the co-pilot – an Omani national whom the Journal named as Hamam al-Hammami, citing people briefed on the investigation – was hired by flydubai, which allowed him to fly on the sensitive route between the United Arab Emirates and Israel. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired in the Emirates. The Omani and UAE governments and flydubai were contacted for comment, the outlets reported.



The co-pilot was born in the UAE to an Omani father and Syrian mother and has spent several years of his life in the UAE, CNN reported, adding that an Israeli official also confirmed his identity though the outlet has not named him. A now-deleted LinkedIn profile under the name Hamam al-Hammami said he worked at Oman Air for seven years, leaving in February 2025, before joining Morocco’s Royal Air Maroc from June 2025 to January 2026. While the profile did not mention flydubai, a source confirmed to CNN that it belonged to the suspect. People disembark from the flydubai flight after it made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. AP The profile only had two posts, CNN reported, both made about nine hours after the flydubai incident. It is unclear who published the posts or whether they were scheduled in advance. One of the posts included a video showing planes and then a photograph of Ayman al-Zawahiri, who led al-Qaeda after the death of Osama Bin Laden. The second post featured an AI-generated image depicting Islam’s three holiest sites Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem, CNN reported.



About the same time, the same posts appeared on an Instagram account bearing the same name, before that account was also deleted. Related Article Updated

Aviation ‘Islamist radical’: Israel claims horror flight co-pilot shared hate online The co-pilot was arrested on Wednesday after flight FZ1073 – carrying 182 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv – made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The motive for the alleged attack is now under investigation and the suspect has been handed over to the UAE, which is leading the probe. Israel said on Thursday that the suspect was said to have undergone an “Islamist radical indoctrination” in the first formal indication of a motive for a midair emergency likened to the 9/11 attacks in the US. Meanwhile, the Indian captain who helped thwart the apparent attempt to crash the plane flight described how he fought for his life in the minutes after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent.



Captain Smit Machchhar, recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call broadcast live on television news channels that he knew he had to get back on his feet to save the passengers aboard the aircraft. “I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” he said from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.” Machchhar, who is from India’s financial hub of Mumbai, was seriously injured in Wednesday’s attack but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and restrain the attacker as the Boeing 737 descended sharply, witnesses and Israeli authorities said. He has been hailed as a hero for his actions, with world leaders saying he helped prevent a disaster.



Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attacker was arrested in Saudi Arabia. His motive for the attack was not immediately clear. Saudi Arabia later said he had been handed over to the United Arab Emirates. Related Article Visual story

Aviation A terrifying plunge, loud screams, blood everywhere: How flight FZ1073 unfolded, moment by moment Modi told Machchhar his “courage, patience, and presence of mind” saved many lives. Machchhar said his flying experience allowed him to sense the plane’s steep descent even after he was knocked down by the attacker. “I have been flying planes for 17 years and serving as a captain for the last 11 years. I can sense exactly what is happening with the aircraft even with my eyes closed. When I was down, I could feel that the aircraft was plummeting,” he said.



Machchhar said that during those difficult moments, he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a Hindu devotional hymn dedicated to Lord Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage. “Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” he told Modi. Machchhar, who is married and has two children, has worked for flydubai for about four years, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before joining the airline, he spent 11 years with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier, where he served as a senior commander and line training captain. He logged more than 9750 flying hours with SpiceJet. In his first public comments on the incident, flydubai chief executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said on Friday that authorities were conducting an official investigation, supported by the airline, after what he described as a “safety incident” in the cockpit. “It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts,” he said in a written statement, acknowledging that there were “many questions” about what happened on flight FZ1073.



Philip Kean, chief executive of Mainland Air Services, the New Zealand flight school where Machchhar trained, said pilots were taught how to take over if a fellow crew member becomes incapacitated. But the training does not typically prepare them for a stabbing attack by a colleague, he told The Associated Press on Friday. “I don’t think there’s much in the handbook for being stabbed,” Kean said. “You’re friends and you’re flying together,” he said. “Nobody would expect … a person to have a go at you like that.” AP, Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
