The Cats flew out of the gates after half-time, dominating the inside 50 count and ballooning their lead by 29 points at three-quarter time.

Richmond was kept scoreless in the final term as the visitors cruised to victory.

AAP

World.title: Tedesco and Ponga went through different worlds to meet in NRL grand final
World.content:
Sunday's NRL grand final between the Roosters and Newcastle is a land of contrasts and nowhere is more apparent than the difference between the two fullbacks and captains, James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga.

Their position, status and ability is about all the two have in common and right from the start the two have walked very different paths to Stadium Australia.

Ponga has been in the papers since he was 15, his first highlights went viral when he was only 17, his first NRL game was a sudden-death semi-final and his first touch was a scorching linebreak that announced a new prince was born.

Once he joined Newcastle in 2018 and finished as the Dally M runner up in his first full season in first grade, his talent was so blinding he never had to prove himself — belief was in his ability was assured.

The world was his, because everyone in rugby league was so eager to give it to him.

For the 33-year old Tedesco, things were different. The Camden product was a good junior, but far from a great one. Just making first grade was far from a guarantee.

Eventually, he didn't just run down those who were ahead of him, he raced right past them and by the time he made his NRL debut for Wests Tigers in Round 1 of the 2012 season he'd shown himself to be a player of the future.

But that future would have to wait. Where Ponga's debut was covered in chrome, Tedesco's became the hardest day of his young life when he blew his knee out 30 minutes in and was stretchered off Leichhardt Oval in tears.

It kicked off a series of injury troubles and it wasn't until three seasons later that Tedesco managed to shrug them off and become an every-week first grader.

During those years, the naysayers rose up and once again Tedesco outlasted them. He is a player of enormous internal motivation — for him, improvement is less of a journey to be better than a compulsion that defines him and he has put a saddle on that beast and ridden it to greatness.

Tedesco suffered a serious knee injury in his NRL debut. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The doubt of others is the whip he uses to flog it, like he did when time seemed to come for him as he lost his New South Wales and Australian spots two years ago.

He was old enough to go quietly into that good night without shame, and after a career of magnificent achievement the game was prepared to move on only Tedesco would not let it.

"In 2024 and 2025 when I wasn't playing Origin or Test footy, people were doubting me a bit and I got some drive from that," said Tedesco.

Tedesco defies time en route to record Dally M triumph Roosters fullback James Tedesco held off the challenge of players over a decade his junior to defy time and claim his second Dally M player of the year award.

"I've been used to that — growing up I was told I wasn't going to make it when I wasn't picked in teams, when I had injuries at the start of my career people told me my body wouldn't last.

"Those external things do motivate me, but the internal one is still the biggest. That'll always be there for me and when it isn't I'll realise it's time to finish."

It had been so long since he was counted out but Tedesco still fought like a demon to prove himself one more time as he claimed last year's Dally M medal and returned to Origin this season.

It has given him a second life but it's still not enough. He is not satisfied and doubts he ever will be.

"I'll never be happy with my game. I always want to improve and learn and get better," said Tedesco.

"That's a part of me, that's been ingrained in me since I was a kid. It's got me to where I am today."

At 33, Tedesco is still one of the best players in the competition. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

Tedesco has been in that place for many years and that is where Ponga now strides towards.

Right from those first days in Newcastle his raw star power, through no fault of his own, quickly made him bigger than the club he played for.

The adulation continued to flow like a river as the highlights and the Fox League spots stacked up as personal success came naturally to Ponga, but in terms of team success there were many lean winters.

The 29-year old didn't play in a final until 2020, didn't win one until 2023 and in the last three weeks the Knights have more finals victories than the rest of Ponga's time with the club combined.

Ponga has carried the weight of expectations his entire career. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

What seemed like a pre-destined journey to the top has not always been smooth. But if Ponga could speak to his younger self he wouldn't ask him to change because if he did it might not have brought him to where he is right now.

"He'd have wanted it earlier, he was impatient. But it makes it sweeter, to go through those tough times — the adversity, injuries, bad years," said Ponga.

"All the emotion came out when Sandon (Smith) took that intercept. But I wouldn't trade any of it because I'm grateful to be here now.

"There was a lot of tension. I think everyone was riding that last minute with us. The relief — nine years I've been here and I've always dreamt of being in this position and it came true with that intercept."

Emotion has been the driving force of Newcastle's run to the grand final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Ponga's uncontainable passion as a leader has been vibrant and bustling and it's come through in his football, which has perhaps been better but has never been tougher.

He has not scored a try or set one up in this finals series even as he's been outstanding in all three matches, with his running game, defence and leadership coming to the fore.

"When you grow up, you mature — or you'd hope so. The environment I'm in has changed, it allows me to be the best version of myself and it allows me to be myself," said Ponga.

"There's no pressure on me to be someone I'm not, as a player or a person. Justin (Holbrook) has done that and this playing group has done that."

The raw and bleeding edge Ponga has showed is a far cry from his younger days, when sometimes he could be a little too relaxed for his own good.

It helped him carry the weight of a city, a club and a game that expected so much of him, but other times it came to the surface in ways that did not befit a player of his stature — most notably when he said a strawberry thickshake lifted his spirits after coach Nathan Brown was sacked in 2019.

"Off the field, early in his career, he'd probably admit he was a bit lackadaisical. He was cruisy, he'd kick back," said Bradman Best, who first played alongside him that season.

"Now he holds everyone accountable, he drives standards. He's having an impact on other people.

"He's found that balance between staying calm and firing up."

Ponga has led from the front to take Newcastle to the brink of a premiership. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Young prop Cody Hopwood, who was just 11 years old when Ponga first came to town and knows him only as he is now, puts it best.

"He doesn't try and overdo the role, he doesn't try to be someone he's not," said Hopwood.

"He's Kalyn Ponga and that's enough."

The Roosters always expect to be in grand finals so on some level they knew they could be here but the Knights have known it as well, as long ago as the old days of about three weeks ago.

Plenty said they'd never get anywhere, but now we know that they knew better and while Ponga has envisioned lifting the premiership trophy plenty of times before it's only in the last two weeks that it's come into sharper focus.

Newcastle rises as one ahead of grand final Ahead of their first grand final in a generation, Newcastle is ready to hold the Knights closer to their hearts than ever before as team and city show why they are one.

"You do it nearly every day because it gives you a purpose. It's why you wake up and train so hard, it's why you dedicate yourself to this, it's why you put your body through things you shouldn't," said Ponga.

"But it didn't become a reality until after the Warriors, before that it was just a thought."

Ponga's love for his club and his town is palpable and that's important because it hasn't always been so.

Over the years there have been whispers of moves to Sydney — the Roosters were always meant to be in the mix, even with Tedesco — or of a possible move to rugby, plus a serious flirtation with the Dolphins when they were entering the competition.

But earlier this season he signed for another four years on a watertight contract with none of the clauses or flexibility he's had in the past.

It was a show of faith that has been rewarded and since his transformation from a great player who plays for the Knights into a great Knight and now he is Newcastle, forever and always, no matter what.

"We're in it and to see it, to feel it, it's inspiring. It's everything you ever dreamt of," said Ponga.

"I'm proud to be a part of this club. I'm proud to lead these boys. I'm proud to be a part of this community."

A grand final win will be a moment for ascension for Ponga's nine years with the club and he has moved to the edge of paradise because he has been able to fuse the internal and external motivations as Tedesco has long done.

At 33, Tedesco still holds his club's premiership fate in his hands. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar )

For Tedesco and his Roosters it's a bit simpler. Having slayed the latest demons, he wants to take the feelings out of the grand final as best he can.

Their key is to keep this as a football game rather than a holy war, to be as calm in the face of overwhelming passion as Ponga once was.

"Just the other night I found myself thinking about the game almost too much, thinking about moments and what could happen," said Tedesco.

"I had to get away from that, because I didn't want to play too early. But it's not about the result, it's about the performance and the process.

"It's easier to say that than it is to do it, but that's something I have to instil into the boys.

"Be proud of where we are, but know the job isn't finished."

World.title: Man City appeals guilty findings of breaking EPL's financial rules
World.content:
Manchester City has filed an appeal against an independent commission ruling that found the club guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, seeking to overturn the verdict and avoid potentially severe sanctions.

The league said on Tuesday that ​City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million ($1.71 billion) over nearly a decade.

City was found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league's financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as three out of four charges concerning failures to cooperate with the investigation.

The club has denied wrongdoing throughout the process.

"Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026 the Club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter," the club said in a statement.

"The Club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case."

The appeal will be heard by an independent three-member appeal board appointed by the chair of the league's Judicial Panel.

"The club lodged the appeal to the Chair of the Judicial Panel," the league said in a statement.

"The independent Appeal Board hearing will remain private and confidential until publication of the outcome is permitted."

Appeal decision is final

The Premier League's rules state that an appeal hearing should be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing concluding.

The appeal will take place in private, as did the original hearings. The board will review the commission's decision, but will not conduct a full rehearing of the case.

The board can dismiss the appeal, allow it, refer the case back to the commission for further consideration or alter any sanction or compensation order imposed.

A decision by the appeal board is final and cannot be challenged further except in limited circumstances that permit a subsequent arbitration process.

With potential sanctions including heavy fines, points deductions and other sporting penalties, and with relegation or the removal of titles also discussed as possible outcomes, the case could have consequences across the league.

City can also separately appeal against any sanctions. It remains unclear whether sanctions will be announced before the appeal is heard, and whether they would take effect immediately.

A league representative told Reuters they could not discuss the process for confidentiality reasons.

While the fate of the case remains unresolved, the season will continue, with leaders City looking for their sixth straight league win when they visit Liverpool on October 11.

Reuters

World.title: NRLW needs its own CEO, says legend Ali Brigginshaw
World.content:
In her final press conference before retirement, rugby league legend Ali Brigginshaw has called on the NRL to create a separate chief executive for the women's game.

As she prepares for a fairytale finish hoping to win back-to-back premierships with Brisbane, Brigginshaw knows the NRLW still has much growing to do.

At today's official pre-grand final press conference, the Bronco was asked to put herself at the desk of newly crowned executive chairman Peter V'landys.

"If there's someone in charge of the [women's] game, maybe someone that plays the game, not me, maybe Millie," Brigginshaw joked about her fellow retiring grand finalist, the Roosters' Millie Elliott.

"Just someone that knows the game and what we've been through.

"We try to shape our game exactly [how] the men do, but there's nothing saying we have to just follow in those footsteps.

"We can go in a different direction, we can do what we want to do and what's best for the [NRLW] players and the staff."

Ali Brigginshaw was given a guard of honour for Brisbane's last home game. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

The women's game is currently managed by the chief executive of the NRL. In contrast, the AFLW has always had its own dedicated leadership, currently headed by Laura Kane.

It was not the only major innovation suggested at today's fan event, with tributes to Brigginshaw also on the agenda.

"She will be remembered in the game for such a long time, and I really hope that they name an award after Ali," Broncos coach Scott Prince said.

The 2020 Dally M medallist has captained her state and country and now leaves behind a legacy that even her fiercest rivals admire.

"Ali's been a pioneer of our game for a very long time now, and I've been really lucky to know Ali for a number of years and play with her and experience her as a leader as well," Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly said.

Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly paid credit to the retiring Ali Brigginshaw. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

She also shared plenty of praise for her own retiring teammates Corban Baxter and Elliott, the 2022 Dally M medallist.

"[Millie] never stops; she's always putting her best foot forward. She promotes the game in such a positive and respectful light that so many young girls look up to.

"Corban, she's the most humble, beautiful human that I think has just put such a landmark on this game."

Meanwhile, the Roosters will make a last-second decision on winger Jayme Fressard as she races the clock to have her shoulder right for grand final day.

The Blues representative picked up a shoulder injury in last week's win over Canberra and did not return to the field after half-time.

A final decision will be made after the captain's run tomorrow, with coach John Strange rating Fressard a "50-50" chance of playing.

"A little niggle, a few fitness tests to still get through, but hopefully looking good," Strange said.

"I just really want to be present this week and do everything that I need to do to be the best athlete as possible."

AAP

World.title: Amy Shark to lead NRL grand final musical tribute to Jai Arrow
World.content:
An all-star ensemble of Australian musicians is set to take part in this weekend's NRL grand final pre-game entertainment.

Pop sensation Amy Shark is leading the performance, alongside members from Newcastle favourites and Better hit-makers The Screaming Jets, electronic duo Peking Duk, plus rock groups Grinspoon, and Teen Jesus and the Jean Teasers.

The all-Australian supergroup will soundtrack an on-ground tribute to South Sydney Rabbitohs player Jai Arrow, who told ABC earlier this week he knew "nothing" about plans for him to take a lap of honour around Stadium Australia on Sunday.

The ABC understands that Shark, who performed at the 2020 NRL grand final, and company will perform a series of cover songs, including the Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.

Each musician's appearance fee is reportedly being donated to motor neurone disease causes.

The Screaming Jets were among the acts speculated by fans to replace Tones And I. (Supplied: The Screaming Jets)

News of the supergroup musical tribute comes after the NRL's negotiations to secure Tones And I fell through, leaving the grand final without a pre-match entertainment headliner.

Why Tones And I won't appear at grand final Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred on the NRL's insistence that she perform her 2019 mega-hit Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

However, the musician's team confirmed that prior commitments touring with Macklemore in the US left her unable to accept the offer when it was made in September.

"Nothing was signed or confirmed in writing," Tones and I's management said.

"Due to the last-minute nature and prior commitments by Tones, we were unable to accept the offer."

It sparked speculation over potential replacements for pre-match entertainment, including Silverchair frontman Daniel Johns ruling out rumours that the band would be reuniting to cheer on their home team, the Newcastle Knights

Jai Arrow was awarded the Provan-Summons Medal at the 2026 Dally M Awards for embodying the spirit of the game. (Getty Images: Don Arnold/WireImage)

Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment — running close to $1 million — could be put to better use.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend $1 million on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

"You spend money to get outcomes, and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league."

Peter V’landys said money set aside for pre-match entertainment would be invested in junior rugby league. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

V'landys also said the league would be donating $100,000 to Arrow's family, following the Rabbitohs player's departure from the NRL earlier this year after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease.

The grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop star Teddy Swims last year, and previous acts such as Billy Idol and Tina Turner.

"Our game sells itself," said V'landys.

"People come to watch rugby league. They don't come to watch a pop concert."

World.title: How Assefa ran third fastest marathon ever despite 'destroyed' Achilles
World.content:
Right up until the 40km mark of the Berlin Marathon at the weekend, Tigst Assefa was well on track to regain her world record.

After 10km, the Ethiopian star was already over a minute in the lead of a race that quickly became a challenge between her and the clock.

By the 30km mark, the noted fast-finisher was running inside world record pace and flying.

"She was on [target] to run 2:09:30, 2:09:40," Assefa's representative Gianni Demadonna told The Associated Press on Tuesday.

Tigst Assefa was flying through the first 30km of the race, running well under world record pace. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

Official World Marathon Majors social media accounts were excitedly posting "this is on" with Assefa 20 seconds under the existing world record time, set by controversial Kenyan Ruth Chepng'etich.

Chepng'etich's record is 2:09:56 from the 2024 Chicago Marathon, but she hasn't raced since July 2025 after admitting to a doping violation.

She is currently serving a three-year ban. There is no suggestion that Chepng'etich doped in Chicago and that record still stands.

Assefa was within touching distance of eliminating Chepng'etich from the record books.

But, within sight of the Brandenburg Gate at just 2 kilometres remaining, Assefa began to grimace, then started to limp and hobbled to the line.

She eventually finished 68 seconds shy of Chepng'etich's record.

Assefa suffered 'complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon'

Assifa's finishing time of 2:11:04 was the third-fastest in history and gave the Olympic silver medallist her third career victory in Berlin, in a new course record.

But incredibly, it was later revealed that the 29-year-old had suffered a "complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon" and has since undergone surgery.

According to her team, Assefa had felt pain in her Achilles from the 31st kilometre, but pushed on regardless, before complete disaster struck with just 2km to go.

Tigst Assefa was unable to stand after crossing the line. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Andreas Gora)

The Achilles tendon connects your calf muscles to your heel bone and lifts the heel when the calf muscle contracts.

"Your Achilles is basically a spring to propel yourself forward," Zoe Russell, a specialist sports and exercise physio as awarded by the Australian College of Physiotherapists, told ABC Sport.

"It transfers your load to propel you forward.

"Tendon experts around the world sort of suggest that a painful tendon doesn't often rupture because it just can't sustain the load.

"You don't typically hear this story of how they're running along, they're sore and then it pops."

How can you run with a ruptured Achilles?

Associate Professor Peter Malliaras, a physiotherapist and clinical researcher at Monash University, told ABC Radio National's Health Report in 2022 that an Achilles tendon rupture "is quite a catastrophic injury".

"It will prevent you from pretty much doing everything in your daily functions; including walking, running, driving, for a fair period of time," he said.

Tigst Assefa could barely struggle to her feet. (Getty Images: Anadolu/Halil Sagirkaya)

Demadonna claimed that Assefa "completely destroyed the tendon" by the end of the race, running the final 500 metres without it.

"She was no longer able to run, because when she was going to put her foot on the ground she had no power," Demadonna said.

Adidas one-run-and-done shoe sets new mark in sport's arms race Adidas's new running shoe helped Ethiopia's Tigst Assefa take more than 2 minutes off the marathon world record in Berlin at the weekend — but if you want to get hold of the one-run-and-done shoe, you'd better start saving.

Yet Assefa was still able to finish the race, running along at a fair lick too, despite being unable to push off with her forefoot.

One reason for her ability to keep moving forward could be found in the super shoes she was wearing, with the integrated carbon plate essentially providing some of the spring instead.

"It could have helped her keep going, yes," Russell suggested.

"Those carbon plates will allow you to transfer your load a bit easier."

Nevertheless, Assefa collapsed soon after crossing the line in clear distress before support arrived, including Ethiopian long-distance running legend Haile Gebrselassie.

Quick surgery vital

She was immediately flown to Munich by private jet courtesy of her sponsor, Adidas, where Demadonna said she underwent "very complex surgery" on Monday.

Without knowing the exact details of the rupture, or the exact surgery technique used, Russell said a time frame for a return would be impossible to guess, but noted that quick surgery was essential.

"Things can move quickly, really quickly in elite sport," she said.

"I've had athletes get an appointment with a surgeon within 20 minutes, half an hour of the injury.

Tigst Assefa was aided by four-time Berlin winner Haile Gebrselassie to leave the finishing area. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

"When you've got means and connections at the elite level, things can move very quickly — and you do want to move fairly quickly with an Achilles rupture because it is constantly under tension. When it ruptures, it actually retracts back.

"So if you're waiting weeks for surgery, it means that your muscles actually start to suffer the effects of de-conditioning and it retracts, which makes for a technically harder surgical process because you've got to pull it and put it all on tension and then stitch it up.

"For an elite athlete, you'd want to get it in two or three days, whereas in the general population, you'll probably get away with getting it within a week."

In a statement, Assefa's coach Gemedu Dedifo said that she "successfully underwent surgery" within 24 hours.

"Tigst is a champion," the statement read.

"We believe in her strength, courage and determination.

"We look forward to seeing her recover and return to the track and roads."

Assefa vows to return

Assefa sent a message from her hospital bed via the Berlin Marathon organisers, defiantly promising to return to break the record.

"My surgery went well," she said in a statement.

"I am overwhelmed by the tremendous support I have received from all over the world. From the bottom of my heart, I would like to thank everyone for their incredible support and concern.

"I will definitely come back to Berlin, and then I will break the world record."

Tigst Assefa holds the women's only world record. (Getty Images: Xinhua/Li Ying)

No marathon has seen more world records than Berlin, with 13 set at the race since 1974 thanks to its largely flat profile with just 73 metres of elevation gain and 79 metres of elevation loss over the 42km.

Assefa set one of those world records in 2023, running 2:11:53 to become the first woman to set a record on the course since Sydney Olympic champion Naoko Takahashi did so in 2001.

Assefa already holds the women's only world record, having run 2:15:41 to win the 2026 London Marathon in April.

Races where men and women start at the same time, as is the case in Berlin, tend to be faster for women, who are able to benefit from male pacemakers who can block the wind and reduce fatigue earlier in the race.

Tech.title: Meta open sources code to let you make Muse AI gadgets
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced. The company suggests projects like loading Muse on a color E Ink display to show reminders, adding it to an HDMI stick so you can display Muse on a big screen, or putting Muse on a small touchscreen device to make what looks kind of like a DIY Muse Charm.

“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says. “Program an off-the-shelf ESP32 board or set up a Raspberry Pi with our SDKs, then connect Muse to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench.” However, Meta cautions that you should “Proceed at your own risk!”

The company is also giving away a Muse Home Link gadget that it created. With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says. It manufactured 5,000 of the gadgets, according to Meta Superintelligence Labs’ Nat Friedman, and you can claim a waitlist spot for the Muse Home Link now ahead of shipping sometime this month.

Meta’s Muse Home Link gadget. Image: Meta

Tech.title: Netflix is pivoting away from prestige
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

Many of Netflix’s biggest critically acclaimed hits have been the products of its multiyear production deals with noted directors like David Fincher and Shawn Levy. In the past few weeks, though, the streamer has brought some of those partnerships to an end in a way that feels indicative of a larger strategic shift. With rival studios Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery on the verge of a megamerger that will reshape the entertainment landscape, Netflix is clearly thinking about how it can continue to hold its own in the ongoing streaming wars. But as the company charts its path forward, its plan to court subscribers might not put so much emphasis on big-name moviemakers.

On Thursday, Netflix shared that its production deal with David Fincher is coming to an end after six years. First announced in 2020, the partnership — which was originally scheduled to last for four years — gave Netflix the exclusive streaming rights to Fincher’s then-upcoming projects like his Herman J. Mankiewicz biographical drama, Mank. With Fincher having previously executive produced original series for Netflix like House of Cards and Mindhunter, the deal seemed to be a sign of Netflix having faith in his ability to keep audiences riveted.

At the time, Fincher joked that Mank’s critical reception and box office performance before it began streaming would determine what kinds of projects Netflix would let him make. Critics generally praised the film and it was ultimately nominated for 10 Academy Awards — two of which it won. But during Mank’s three-week theatrical run, it only made around $100,000 against a $25 million budget, and once it hit Netflix, it only managed to spend a single day on the streamer’s list of its top 10 most-watched movies (in last place). Though Fincher’s next project for Netflix — 2023’s The Killer — debuted at No. 1 on the chart, the project’s $452,000 box office gross against a $175 million budget made it another financial dud. And with The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth set to show in theaters for two weeks before it hits Netflix on December 23rd, the film could be another example of Fincher delivering a movie that isn’t exactly a huge monetary win for the streamer.

Fincher’s track record with Netflix is somewhat similar to director Shawn Levy’s. After almost a decade of working exclusively with the streamer on projects including Stranger Things, The Adam Project, and Shadow and Bone, Levy announced last month that he had signed a new overall production deal with Disney. Levy — whose directing career began with a number of Disney Channel series — framed his decision to leave Netflix as a kind of homecoming. But it was hard not to see his jumping ship as having been prompted by the way Stranger Things’ final season left audiences and critics disappointed.

The same was true when Stranger Things co-creators Matt and Ross Duffer announced last August 2025 that they were leaving Netflix for a four-year TV / film production deal with Paramount. The brothers could still have a hand in future Stranger Things projects, and their next series — The Boroughs — debuted on Netflix this past May to respectable numbers. But just one month after its release, The Boroughs was canceled.

In a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said that Levy’s and the Duffer Brothers’ departures were driven by the filmmakers’ desire to spend more time working on feature-length projects. Levy’s Star Wars: Starfighter is slated to premiere next May, and the Duffers’ untitled Paramount film will debut sometime in 2028. Though Sarandos framed the filmmakers’ exits in a positive light, they’re part of a larger trend that makes it seem like Netflix is moving on from its era of signing filmmakers to lengthy deals. The company has also parted ways with Marriage Story writer-director Noah Baumbach, whose other Netflix projects, like White Noise and Jay Kelly, failed to make much of a splash.

Going forward, it seems like Netflix’s main game plan is to put an increased focus on producing lower-budget series, live events, and sports programming. The company obviously isn’t giving up on movies — Gerwig will direct another Narnia feature and there’s a KPop Demon Hunters sequel on the way — but episodic content has been shown to be much more effective at keeping subscribers coming back.

This is why we’ve recently seen Netflix hyping up strange reality shows like Squid Game: The Challenge, Wonka’s The Golden Ticket, and The New Stanford Prison Experiment. None of those shows exactly come across as must-see TV like the horror series Mike Flanagan produced for Netflix before Amazon poached him in 2022. But that may not matter to Netflix as long as people are watching. After years of spending millions of dollars to produce movies that did not always result in consistent subscriber growth, Netflix appears to be entering a period of making more conservative bets. That might make the service feel a little less premium than it has in the past, but it could help it live to fight another day.

Tech.title: Apple will limit Mac disk access as AI agents ‘substantially’ increase risk
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple will add new limits for “full disk access” on Mac in response to risks posed by AI agents, as reported earlier by TechCrunch. In an update on Friday, Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

The change comes just weeks after Inc’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages, despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone pushed back on this report, saying access to Messages is “entirely opt-in.” Stone added that you have to “enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content.”

Now Apple is addressing how developers use that sweeping access, saying:

Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding… As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially.

Full disk access is a permission on macOS that gives an app access to a user’s entire system. Apple says the feature “largely sidesteps” privacy controls offered to users “to allow backup apps to function properly on Mac.” The company doesn’t say when it plans to roll out its update for full disk access. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Tech.title: Sling TV drops its one-day cable passes
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Dish-owned Sling TV will no longer be offering its Sling Pass feature that allowed people to buy a single day of cable TV programming at a time, as reported by The Desk.

The feature was announced last year and offered a day pass, a weekend pass, and a week-long pass option to be able to watch channels like ESPN and CNN without a full-month cable subscription. But soon after it launched, Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery sued Sling TV over Sling Pass, though a federal judge ruled against Disney in its request for a preliminary injunction to block the feature.

“Sling was built to give our customers the ultimate control over their entertainment, and Sling Passes delivered on that promise for millions,” Sling TV says in a statement on its website. “Though Sling Passes are no longer available, we look forward to continuing to innovate and showing our customers new ways to experience the content they love.” The Desk also reports that the note was sent to customers.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s Dot agent is enterprise software that can also order your dinner
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over a decade of experience writing about consumer tech. She has a special interest in mobile photography and telecom. Previously, she worked at DPReview.

It’s a tale as old as last week: OpenAI’s new agent platform, called Dots, is full of cute little guys who can do your bidding.

But unlike the ultra-approachable Meta Muse, Dots feel very much like using workplace software that happens to be able to order you a burrito — emphasis on work.

OpenAI announced Dots earlier this week. Like Muse, Dots have blobby, anthropomorphic avatars and customizable names. In the future, OpenAI says you’ll be able to have multiple Dots, but right now you get one. I named mine Dotty McDotface.

The interface looks similar to Muse’s; you chat with the agent in one window and follow its work in another as it clicks around on a virtual machine. But Dots are less personal shoppers, even though they can help you buy stuff. They’re more like coworkers: business software that can use other software. Your Dot’s virtual machine can access apps like Blender and GIMP right off the bat. You can also give it access to your own computer through the desktop ChatGPT app, and you can call your Dot if you need to work through things out loud. And OpenAI is offering Dots first to users on its highest-tier accounts, including the $100-per-month Pro account I expensed to test it. Muse and its buzzy competitor Instinct cost you nothing — at least now, and at least until Meta can get it off the ground and presumably start using it to serve you ads, etc. But OpenAI’s gated rollout says a lot about who the product is for, cute avatars notwithstanding.

I’ve been testing other AI agents with day-to-day personal tasks — yielding mixed results — and I was curious how OpenAI’s bot would compare. Despite its more enterprise-y vibes, OpenAI says Dots “can do nearly anything” with its cloud computer and access to apps, so I gave it a shot with some more pedestrian use cases.

To start, I had Dot try to schedule an installation appointment for a new internet service provider at my house (you hear that, Comcast? You’re on notice). It almost got there, and even found a $100 promotional discount in my email that I had mass deleted, but got stuck at a “human check.” Which is problematic for a bot. “This particular check needs a sustained mouse hold that my browser controls don’t support,” it said. “Please open my browser here and hold ‘Press & Hold’ until it completes, then tell me and I’ll continue with installation dates.” I obliged, but it felt a little bit like some teenagers outside of the convenience store asking me to buy them some wine coolers.

I want to know how many meetings Quantum had about adding “(and not a bot)” to this pop-up. Screenshot: The Verge / OpenAI

With my human ability to click and hold a button, Dot got all the way to the checkout screen, where it asked me to input my bank account details. Turns out there’s no slick Stripe integration like Muse has to save your credit card info and use a virtual card for checkout. And in any case, the new provider needed my bank account to get a $5 discount on my bill every month. Dot paused to let me enter the numbers into the virtual browser; I didn’t trust it well enough to punch in my checking account number and decided to just do it all myself on my own computer. Not exactly a spectacular start.

I gave Dot a few other personal tasks, and the results were mixed. It couldn’t find the option for a free tour and entry at a coworking space I’ve been meaning to try out, and instead offered to sign me up for a $35 day pass. I had Instinct’s agent, which I’ve also been testing, look for the trial option; it found it and set up an appointment within minutes. “Why did you miss this option?” I questioned Dot over the phone after the incident. “I jumped to the wrong conclusion,” it said. I hung up.

I’m going to start calling this the Teriyaki Test. Screenshot: The Verge / OpenAI

Later, I had it try to retrieve some information in my Ikea account about a hanging planter I bought. It reported that it was unable to log in to my Ikea account because it got stuck in a looping security check. Elsewhere on the internet, the neighborhood teriyaki spot wouldn’t allow Dot onto its ordering page. Something about Dot’s footprint seems to get it tripped up on security checks more often than Muse or Instinct; Dot offered a link to OpenAI’s page about websites blocking its cloud browser traffic as an explanation. Whatever the reason, it required more manual input and browser takeovers than other AI agents, possibly because it wasn’t purpose-built for ordering teriyaki or handling your Ikea returns.

I really saw Dot come into its element when I gave it access to something fully within my control: my personal website. It is embarrassingly outdated and I asked Dot to pull together a new, more streamlined design. It did, and when I sat down to type out some changes I want made for the next version, I thought, “To hell with it. I’ll just give it a call.” I hashed out the changes I wanted section by section over 10 minutes, walked away to do some dishes, and got a ping that the next iteration was ready for me to review. Not perfect, but better. Once again, AI proves most helpful when you give it a large dataset (me rambling for 10 minutes) it can turn into something useful. I carried out a few more rounds of iterations chatting with Dot in a browser window on my computer and using voice-to-text on the phone app as I walked around the house cleaning up Brio train tracks and stuffies.

Something about Dot’s footprint seems to get it tripped up on security checks more often than Muse or Instinct

Dot made a lot more sense once I gave it access to my computer. There, I gave it two tasks: Put together a handful of video files on my desktop featuring a TV hit I did into one clip sized properly for social media, and deploy the changes to my personal website that we had worked through in a prototype. I had to give it a shocking number of permissions, but it worked. I watched it click around the website backend and re-create the prototype block by block. I walked away from the computer and got updates on the ChatGPT app on my phone — the consolidated video clip was ready, which I reviewed while I drank a coffee. It was the most Silicon Valley I’ve ever felt in my life.

I absolutely could have figured out how to put all those clips together myself. In fact, I did the first time around, but it looked janky and was too big to upload on any social media website. Dot did a much better job and I had a clip to share within minutes. It handled the website update, too. The new design is basic, but it’s miles ahead of the complicated, out-of-date version I’d been rocking until yesterday. Gotta hand it to Dotty McDotface.

Helping you update a website while ordering dinner is the AI agent future we were promised. Screenshot: The Verge / OpenAI

Dot makes a lot more sense when you think of it and use it as “Codex, but for regular people” — a cute little blob that can take care of some part of your business while you do other things. Where the more personal AI agents like Muse feel like glorified autofill and a universal online shopping cart, Dot seems like a harbinger of the future of work.

Or a future of work. Presumably, since you pay for it upfront, it won’t be subject to the kind of monetization pressure as Muse and Instinct eventually will, which makes sense for enterprise software. Nobody wants to be nagged by AI while they work. That is, assuming you do the kind of work that AI can help you with, and you trust OpenAI to do it. Big caveats!

It helped me out with some tasks that, if I’m being honest, I would have just not gotten around to doing. That’s pretty handy. But I don’t think it’s $100-a-month handy, at least in my line of work. I can see how it would be much more useful to someone like our friend Casey Newton, who’s in the thick of launching a new business.

And with some help logging into my Uber Eats account, it did actually order my teriyaki in the end.

Tech.title: Breaking up (with Elon Musk) is hard to do
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In a throwback to MySpace-style internet drama, Shivon Zilis announced that she and the father of her four children, Elon Musk, had broken up on X.

To do so, she quote-tweeted a post from “Big Tech Alert,” an account that, among other things, monitors what accounts are following and unfollowing each other. That post noted Musk was no longer following her on X. It was also sponsored by Kalshi, because everything in this relationship is totally fucking cursed, dude.

In her statement, Zilis wrote, “It’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week with no warning, but that’s just how it is sometimes.”

“Uh, you know.”

Zilis, in addition to her romantic, uh, entanglement with Musk, also served as… well, she denied under oath that she was his chief of staff but says she worked across Musk’s “entire AI portfolio: Tesla, Neuralink, and OpenAI” during a trial earlier this year, in which Musk sued Sam Altman — long story, there’s some specious legal reasoning but mostly it just looks like punishment for being successful without Musk — over Musk’s donations to OpenAI. During the trial, she claimed to work 80-to-100-hour weeks for Musk, “to go find bottlenecks and solve them.”

Musk apparently had a different view of her role, testifying that she was his chief of staff, and “uh, you know,” prompting loud laughter from the courtroom’s gallery.

Musk’s fixer, Jared Birchall, orchestrates privacy deals for Musk with the baby mamas. Musk has 14 known children.

“Given the tumultuous nature of his early life, his often tortured soul, and how hard he fights for humanity I wanted him to feel the deepest and most stable form of love this world can provide.”

Zilis was a member of OpenAI’s board when she gave birth to twins, though she kept the parentage of the children secret. She only informed her coworkers about having kids with one of their competitors in 2022, after Business Insider reported on court documents listing Musk as the children’s father. Musk lived with her at the time of the testimony.

During her testimony in the case, Zilis appeared to worship Musk, and her breakup post strikes roughly the same tone. “I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,” she wrote. “Given the tumultuous nature of his early life, his often tortured soul, and how hard he fights for humanity I wanted him to feel the deepest and most stable form of love this world can provide.”

The post is so groveling that had I not witnessed her in court, I would have assumed this was some kind of passive-aggressive revenge strategy. Personally, if one of my exes publicly wrote that I was a poor fragile wreck trying to save the world who desperately needed a haven of safety, I would simply die of embarrassment, but God really does make all kinds.

“I’ve loved him more than life itself and he’s taught me 100 lifetimes of knowledge and made my cup overflow with life meaning, so there is a lot of loss, but luckily we created four beautiful little loves of my life,” Zilis wrote.

Last week, Zilis posted about a memoir written by Maye Musk, Elon’s mother: “During tough moments I think about the resilience she’s shown and realize she’s encountered 100x the difficultly I’ve faced and she made it through with grace! It gives me resolve.” I guess we know now what some of the “tough moments” were. “I would highly recommend this book to anyone who wants a beacon of resilience to draw inspiration from,” she added.

Tech.title: Rivian’s sales pop as the company’s big R2 bet starts to pay off
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rivian had high hopes for its more affordable R2 vehicle — and so far, those hopes appear to be paying off.

The company released its third-quarter production and delivery numbers today, reporting 19,751 vehicles produced and 19,248 delivered. That represents an 85 percent year-over-year increase in production and a 45 percent jump in deliveries. (For a direct-to-consumer automaker like Rivian, deliveries serve as a proxy for sales.) The company also reaffirmed its full-year 2026 guidance, expecting to deliver 65,000 to 70,000 vehicles.

Rivian’s sales surge is a rare bright spot in a struggling industry. A year after President Trump and Republicans in Congress eliminated the $7,500 federal EV tax credit, broader EV sales have predictably plunged. According to Cox Automotive, as of September 2026, overall EV sales were down nearly 24 percent year-over-year. Tesla just reported a 2.1 percent decrease in Q3 sales (though that was better than expected).

Rivian has been telling investors it will sell upwards of 25,000 R2s in its first year of production, which would make it one of the fastest launches of a new electric vehicle in US history. The R2 needed to be a hit for Rivian to survive as an independent company. As Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe told us earlier this year: “R2 is the most important thing we have because it’s what takes us from being subscale to being a scaled manufacturer.”

While Rivian doesn’t break down sales by model, the company expects full-year deliveries for both its R1 lineup—the R1T truck and R1S SUV—and its electric delivery van to remain flat. Last year, Rivian delivered over 13,000 vehicles in the third quarter. Assuming R1 and van deliveries held steady, that leaves approximately 6,000 R2 vehicles delivered to customers this quarter.

The sales report comes amid a string of good news for Rivian. The company recently announced that the R2 hit its climate goal of reducing its lifetime emissions by 50 percent four years ahead of schedule.

Tech.title: Beehiiv creators are buzzing about a new price increase
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Beehiiv, a creator platform that has risen in popularity as an alternative to Substack, is increasing its prices — and many users aren’t happy. In a post explaining the increase, Beehiiv cofounder and CEO Tyler Denk says it will allow the company to “continue investing in our core platform experience.”

As part of the change, Beehiiv is changing the name of its midrange Scale plan to Lite, which has gone up by at least $10 per month depending on subscriber count. For someone with up to 10,000 subscribers, for example, Beehiiv will charge $139 / month instead of $109. Meanwhile, the Pro plan (formerly Max) will cost $239 / month for up to 10,000 subscribers, a jump from the previous $219 /month price. Creators with less than 2,500 subscribers can continue using Beehiiv for free.

The price hike has several creators on social media reconsidering their decision to use the platform, which many have joined to avoid the 10 percent cut Substack takes from total subscription revenue. In a post on Bluesky, freelance journalist Tim Stevens expresses frustration with the changes to Beehiiv that he’s seen after switching to the platform earlier this year. “Since then, the sponsor choices and ad rates have tanked.” Stevens writes. “Now, Beehiiv is hiking its fees 25%, making this an even less profitable endeavor.”

Matt Lombardo, who also recently moved his NFL news site Between the Hashmarks from Substack to Beehiiv, mentioned his issues with the change as well. “Beehiiv raising prices without yet offering video podcasts, a viable consistent growth engine on platform, or podcast ads is pretty frustrating to experience, as someone who enjoys the platform,” Lombardo writes on Threads.

Related Writers are fleeing the Substack Tax

In a post on Reddit, Extra Points creator Matt Brown notes that while he believes Beehiiv is a “steal” compared to Substack, he acknowledges that this “really isn’t true for many other publishers,” especially for those who don’t charge a subscription fee for their work:

As these prices increase, I think it’s becoming increasingly clear that if you have under 10K subscribers and rely on Beehiiv to do the majority of your rev-gen, and ESPECIALLY if you’re outside the United States, the answer is going to be No. It isn’t worth it. You’ll be able to get similar functionality at a lower startup cost, and can plug in affilate ads via other networks.

Beehiiv has differentiated itself from other platforms by offering a trove of built-in features, including an integrated ad network, website personalization options, and podcast creation tools. The company recently launched a new feature that allows creators to build a community into their website. “It’s only the second time we’ve ever updated our plans and pricing in beehiiv’s near five year history,” Denk writes. “Over the past several years, we have greatly expanded the capabilities of the platform.”

Tech.title: Meta wants your next gadget to be Muse-infused
Tech.content:
Meta’s Muse, a personal AI agent that books travel, fills out forms, and shops on a user’s behalf, has already proven popular with the masses, but a new side project could be particularly alluring to tinkerers and hackers.

On Friday, the company introduced Muse Gadgets, an open-source project that lets developers build their own hardware that connects to Muse.

Meta is providing open-source firmware (the low-level software that runs a device), and a Linux software development kit (SDK), along with a few project ideas to get users started. These include giving Muse a color e-ink display or loading it onto a stick that plugs into a TV’s HDMI port.

There don’t appear to be many limits, either. Users can set up a low-cost hobbyist computer like a Raspberry Pi or an off-the-shelf ESP32 board, and then connect Muse “to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench,” Meta notes.

The company has also set up a Discord channel to support users.

Meta has already tried the code itself, naturally. Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, said in a post on X that the company built a gadget called Muse Home Link. The USB-C-powered device lets Muse connect to a home network and talk to the smart devices on it, including speakers and smart TVs.

Meta made 5,000 of these Home Links, in fact, and is giving them away for free to Muse subscribers while supplies last, according to Friedman. Considering Friedman’s post about Home Link received nearly 30,000 views in a few hours, we’re guessing those freebies have been claimed. Friedman said Home Link would be ready to ship a few weeks.

Muse Gadgets may not have wide appeal, but it fits nicely into Meta’s all-in strategy to make Muse more than a standalone chatbot. Meta isn’t content to push Muse on everyday consumers; it’s also trying to woo small businesses and enterprises.

The company earlier this week introduced Muse for Small Business, which is free with usage limits and connects Muse to tools such as Shopify, Dropbox, and Slack. It has also launched a new business unit, Meta Enterprise Platform, to help it push its AI offerings to businesses and corporate customers.

Tech.title: Sanders introduces bill to ban the federal government from using Flock
Tech.content:
Flock, whose cameras scan license plates across the country, continues to draw public anger, and now Senator Bernie Sanders wants the federal government out of the business altogether.

Sanders (D-Vermont) on Friday introduced the Ban Flock Act, which would bar federal agencies from using automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) or tapping into data collected by readers run by local police and private companies. Despite its title, the bill doesn’t call out Flock in the text and covers any and all ALPR systems.

The bill allows exceptions only for toll collection and for uses that Congress approves in future legislation, which would have to limit data retention to no longer than 48 hours.

State and local governments would be dinged financially for not complying if the bill became law. (Like most bills, this one faces long odds.) Starting the first fiscal year after enactment, they would lose grants from five federal departments, including the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security, unless they ban the tech.

Americans could also sue the federal government over violations, and state attorneys general could enforce the law.

Flock is the largest ALPR vendor in the U.S., according to Sanders, with more than 120,000 cameras. In a blog post back in February, the company said its network processes more than 20 billion vehicle reads each month.

Under increasing pressure from communities that are protesting the product, suspending their use, and, at an escalating rate, canceling their contracts, Flock has tightened its rules. In August, CEO Garrett Langley, who’d previously said that how police use the cameras is up to local agencies, announced a new default data retention period of seven days, down from 30.

Customers must also now use an audit tool that locks officers out pending review when it flags unusual searches. In one of the highest-profile cases of an officer abusing Flock’s platform, a former Milwaukee officer pleaded guilty to misconduct after searching for his then-partner and her ex 179 times, listing the reason as “investigation.” (During a recent podcast interview, investor Jason Calacanis suggested a “double-key” system in which two people must approve a search, and Langley said the idea is “on the whiteboard.”)

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Senator Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) are co-sponsors.

We’ll be sitting down with Langley at our upcoming Disrupt event, October 13-15 in downtown San Francisco.

Tech.title: Sean Parker is rebuilding Stability AI around music
Tech.content:
In Brief

Sean Parker, the Napster co-founder, has jumped back into the music industry, and he tells The Information that he’s playing by the rules this time. (Asking for forgiveness rather than permission didn’t work out so well last time around, he readily concedes.)

Two years ago, he joined an $80 million rescue of Stability AI, the image-generator startup that nearly collapsed after overspending and internal turmoil led to founder Emad Mostaque’s ouster. Now Parker and his longtime friend Prem Akkaraju, who became CEO, are taking the wraps off what they’ve been building.

The big idea, Parker says, is to turn Stability into the go-to AI toolmaker for music professionals. Toward that end, in late August, the company announced $76 million in funding from, among others, Sony, Warner, and Universal, which also licensed their catalogs for training as part of the deal. Stability has since released three new audio models and AI music-editing software. The AI can generate whole instrumental tracks or short snippets from text prompts. Parker says an upcoming update will let users hum a melody or beatbox a drum pattern to steer it.

Tech.title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents
Tech.content:
Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.

Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.

The decision to limit the Mac feature also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.

AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.

In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.

“Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers.

The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.”

“Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.

Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
